Guariento di Arpo, the same painter who had decorated the Cappella Maggiore of the Eremitani in Padova with the Stories of Saint Augustine, who had also provided the decorative program for the tomb of Doge Giovanni Dolfin in Santi Giovanni e Paolo, and whose earlier frescoes in the Cappella dei Carraresi in the Reggia Carrarese had made him the preeminent painter of the Padovan ruling court, now received from Marco Corner the most prestigious commission in all Venice. The career of Guariento thus serves as a kind of artistic thread that connects the figures in this biographical sequence: the Dolfin tomb, the Eremitani frescoes, and the Palazzo Ducale Paradise are all part of a single pictorial world shaped by one painter across three decades, a painter whose patrons included both the Doge who preceded Corner and Corner himself.

    The Coronation of the Virgin in the Palazzo Ducale also connects explicitly to Guariento's later work documented in 1365 at the Palazzo Ducale in Venice, the same year he was awarded the commission there by the Venetian Republic after Corner's election to the dogeship. In 1365, Guariento was invited by the Venetian Republic to paint a representation of the Coronation of the Virgin in the Palazzo Ducale.

    The figure of Corner's second wife, the Dogaressa Caterina of unknown surname, deserves a brief further consideration, not despite but because of the scarcity of documentation surrounding her. Her low social origins, her "simple habits," and the doge's repeated public defense of her character all suggest a marriage of personal attachment rather than dynastic calculation. In a world where patrician alliances were invariably calculated instruments of family strategy, Corner's marriage to a woman of modest station was genuinely anomalous.

    The doge always loyally defended her and called her a good woman and wife. In the highly codified and performative world of the Venetian patriciate, where public speech was invariably managed and where what a man said about his wife carried institutional implications, this repeated public loyalty to a socially controversial spouse speaks to a dimension of Corner's personality that his official biography does not otherwise illuminate.

    Marco Cornaro died in the early hours of 13 January 1368. He had been doge for two years and nearly six months, old even by the standards of the ducal office, dying at approximately eighty-two years of age.

    He is buried in the Basilica of San Zanipolo, the Basilica dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo, the great Dominican church in the sestiere of Castello that served as the traditional funerary pantheon of the doges of Venice. His tomb stands in the company of those of his immediate predecessors and successors in that extraordinary sequence of Gothic and Renaissance funerary monuments that lines the walls of the nave. His predecessor in the dogeship, Giovanni Dolfin, whose biography immediately precedes this one, also lies in Santi Giovanni e Paolo, as, indeed, do the tombs of Jacopo and Ubertino da Carrara, the Padovan lords whose dynasty was so closely intertwined with the world of Corner's first marriage into the Scrovegni family.

    Corner was succeeded as doge by Andrea Contarini, who would face the gravest military crisis of the century, the War of Chioggia (1378-1381), in which Genoa came perilously close to destroying Venice entirely. Corner himself did not live to see this catastrophe; his reign ended while the economic effects of the Treaty of Zadar were still being felt and before the storm of Chioggia broke. In that sense, his brief dogeship occupies a relatively calm interlude in the turbulence of fourteenth-century Venetian history, a moment of commercial restoration, architectural embellishment, and artistic patronage between the Hungarian war and the Genoese crisis.

    For Alberto's research into the medieval art of the fourteenth century, Marco Corner occupies a particularly rich place. He is the biographical figure who most directly connects the artistic world of Padova, through his Scrovegni marriage and the legacy of Giotto, with the artistic world of Venice, through his commissioning of Guariento for the greatest secular fresco program in the Serenissima's history. He is also the doge who presided over the same moment in which Guariento completed the decorative program for the tomb of Giovanni Dolfin in Santi Giovanni e Paolo, the tomb that Zuleika Murat, whose biography opened this sequence, has studied so meticulously.

    The figure of Guariento thus becomes the artistic axis around which the subjects of these biographies revolve: the Eremitani in Padova, the tomb of Dolfin, and the Coronation of the Virgin in the Palazzo Ducale all bear his hand, all fall within the decade of the 1360s, and all were shaped by the political and cultural world of which Marco Corner was both a product and a principal architect.

  7. Dominic of Guzman (Saint Dominic)

    Dominic of Guzman (1170–1221) was the founder of the Order of Preachers—the Dominicans—and one of the most influential spiritual and intellectual figures of the 13th century, whose impact on theology, art, and medieval culture was immense and enduring. Dominic was born around 1170 in Caleruega, a small village in Old Castile, Spain, to Felice de Guzman and Joanna of Aza, a woman of deep devotion who was later beatified. Tradition holds that before his birth, his mother saw in a dream a dog that, with a torch in its mouth, leaped from her womb and set the world ablaze—an image that became one of the iconographic emblems of the Dominican Order. He completed his studies in Palencia, one of the principal centers of Iberian culture, where he excelled in philosophy and theology, demonstrating from a young age an extraordinary capacity for intellectual synthesis and an uncommon ascetic zeal. Upon completing his studies, Dominic entered the chapter of the Canons Regular of the Cathedral of Osma, where he lived under the Rule of St. Augustine, combining community life with study and prayer. It was precisely in Osma that the decisive turning point of his life began: in 1203, Bishop Diego d'Acevedo took him along on a long diplomatic journey through northern Europe, bound for Denmark, on behalf of King Alfonso VIII of Castile. As they crossed southern France, the two clergymen were confronted with a shocking reality: the widespread prevalence of the Cathar heresy, which had by then conquered entire regions of Languedoc, undermining the social and religious structure of Christian Europe from within. The encounter with Catharism was a revelation and a calling for Dominic. The Cathars—also known as the Albigensians—preached a radical dualism between the material (corrupt) world and the spiritual (pure) world, rejecting the sacraments, the clergy, and the ecclesiastical institution. Their appeal also lay in the exemplary austerity of their ministers, the perfecti, who lived in rigorous poverty, far exceeding that of many Catholic clergy of the time. Dominic immediately understood that the response to heresy could not be merely military repression, but had to come through preaching and the example of his life: he therefore chose to walk the roads of southern France, poor among the poor, publicly debating with the Cathars and seeking to bring them back to the Catholic faith. For a full decade, from 1206 to 1216, Dominic remained in Languedoc as a missionary, collaborating with the Bishop of Toulouse, Folchetto of Marseille. In 1207, he founded a women's monastery at Notre-Dame-de-Prouille, near Fanjeaux, intended to welcome women converted from the Cathar heresy—the first institutional nucleus of the future Dominican family. He refused to participate in the crusade launched by Innocent III against the Albigensians in 1208, remaining faithful to his vocation as a peaceful preacher, even when the papal legate Peter of Castelnau was assassinated and the military crusade devastated the region. In 1215, Dominic gathered a small group of disciples around him in Toulouse and traveled to Rome to obtain papal recognition for the new religious institute. The Fourth Lateran Council, held that same year, had prohibited the founding of new orders, but Innocent III, recognizing the extraordinary value of Dominic's mission, advised him to adopt an existing rule. Dominic chose the Rule of St. Augustine, supplementing it with original constitutions that made theological study and itinerant preaching the pillars of community life. On December 22, 1216, Pope Honorius III solemnly approved the Order of Preachers with the bull Religiosam vitam. The structure Dominic conceived for his order was profoundly innovative: unlike Benedictine monasticism, rooted in a fixed location, the Preachers were by definition itinerant, and their friary was to be located preferably in university cities, alongside the great centers of learning. As early as 1217, Dominic sent his friars to Paris and Bologna—the two principal intellectual centers of Europe—thus inaugurating a model of urban and cultured religiosity that would profoundly shape medieval civilization. In the final years of his life, Dominic traveled tirelessly throughout Italy, Spain, and southern France, founding new monasteries and welcoming a growing number of friars into the Order. In May 1220, he presided over the Order's first General Chapter in Bologna, which drew up the definitive constitutions, establishing precise rules regarding preaching, study, poverty, and the democratic governance of the community. He died in Bologna on August 6, 1221, worn out by fatigue and asceticism, surrounded by his friars. Pope Gregory IX canonized him in 1234, just thirteen years after his death—an exceptionally short time, a sign of the speed with which his holiness was recognized throughout Christendom. St. Dominic's legacy was immense. Within a few decades, his friars became the leading figures of European intellectual life: Thomas Aquinas, Albert the Great, and Meister Eckhart were all Dominicans. In medieval iconography, Dominic is depicted in a white habit and black cloak, holding a lily—a symbol of purity—and with a dog at his feet, in reference to his mother's prophetic dream. His figure was celebrated by Dante in Paradiso (Canto XII), who placed him in the sphere of the Sun alongside St. Francis, presenting him as the champion of the faith, armed with doctrine and preaching. For the scholar of medieval art, the figure of St. Dominic is indispensable: Dominican patronage gave rise to some of the most important pictorial cycles of the Italian 13th and 14th centuries, from Cimabue to Duccio to Guido da Siena, transforming the Order's monasteries into extraordinary workshops of figurative art.

E

  1. Enkleistra (Enkleistra of St. Neophytos)

    The Enkleistra (Greek: Ἐγκλείστρα, from enkleistos, "enclosed" or "shut in") is the term for the cave-hermitage that St. Neophytos the Recluse carved into the hillside above Paphos, Cyprus, beginning in 1159-1160. The word derives from the same root as "enclosure" — it designates the dwelling-place of a recluse, someone who has voluntarily walled themselves off from the world for ascetic, contemplative purposes.

    In Neophytos's case, the Enkleistra was not a single chamber but grew into a small complex of excavated rock-cut cells: his original cell and Bema (the altar space where he could celebrate the liturgy), later expanded with additional cells as his community of disciples grew, and eventually a second, higher cave called the "New Zion," completed by 1197, to which he retreated for greater solitude as the original Enkleistra became more frequented by visitors and pilgrims.

    The term is significant for two reasons. First, it describes a recognized category of Byzantine ascetic dwelling — the cave-hermitage as opposed to a built monastery — though in Neophytos's case the Enkleistra eventually became the core of a fully institutionalized monastery (the still-functioning Monastery of St. Neophytos near Tala, north of Paphos). Second, it is the site of the celebrated fresco cycle painted by Theodoros Apsevdis in 1183, commissioned under the patronage of Bishop Basil Kinnamos — the same cycle that Cyril Mango and Ernest Hawkins studied in their foundational 1966 Dumbarton Oaks Papers article, and that Ioanna Kakoulli and Christian Fischer later subjected to modern materials analysis.

  2. Eremitani

    The church of the Santi Filippo e Giacomo — universally known as the Chiesa degli Eremitani — is a medieval Catholic place of worship that rises in Piazza Eremitani in Padova. Dedicated to Saints Philip and James the Lesser, it was built from 1264 as the church of the Order of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, who maintained their large convent to the north of the church, today occupied by the Musei Civici agli Eremitani. The Augustinian order governed the church until 1806. Today the church holds parish status and is administered by the secular clergy of the Diocese of Padova.

    The Augustinians who built it belonged to the Ordo Fratrum Eremitarum Sancti Augustini, formally consolidated by the Magna Unio of 1256, which merged various congregations of hermits across central and northern Italy under a single mendicant rule. In Padova, two congregations are documented prior to the Magna Unio: the Guglielmiti, established in the Santa Croce area, and the Giamboniti. Their union gave rise to the community that would commission and inhabit the Eremitani complex for over five and a half centuries.

    The initial construction began in 1276 and was completed in 1306. The church was built on the site of an earlier chapel dedicated to Saint Christopher, which was incorporated into the new structure. According to tradition, the construction was carried out under the guidance of Fra' Giovanni degli Eremitani.

    The building is an extraordinary example of the "classicizing" style that developed in Padova during the communal age. Its architectural language features Gothic elements such as pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and flying buttresses, reflecting the transitional period from Romanesque to Gothic architecture.

    The exterior is characterized by the warm tonal contrast between its upper section in exposed terracotta brick — where a handsome central rose window opens — and the lower section, which features a limestone loggia of five arches: the central one frames the main entrance portal, while the lateral ones contained devotional images.

    The interior presents a single nave covered by a distinctive wooden ship's keel ceiling (soffitto a carena), originally the work of Fra' Giovanni degli Eremitani. The walls are adorned with the characteristic alternating bands of red and ochre brick. Despite the devastation of 1944, the spatial structure of the nave still conveys the austere grandeur of the original Gothic design. From an architectural standpoint it is considered one of the finest examples of pure Romanesque in northern Italy.

    One of the most significant functions of the Eremitani in the fourteenth century was its role as a dynastic funerary space for the ruling signoria of Padova, the Da Carrara family. Near the entrance stand two sepulchres sculpted by Andriolo de Santi: on the left, the tomb of Jacopo da Carrara, bearing an inscription composed in Latin couplets by Petrarch; on the right, the tomb of Ubaldino da Carrara. These monuments, respectively dated to approximately 1345 and 1351, were executed by the Venetian sculptor Andriolo de Santi, two other Venetian artists, and the Lombard Bonino da Campione, to whom the two Madonnas and Child in the central niches of the sarcophagi are attributed. Both lords were rulers of Padova in the trecento, and their monuments — transported here from the destroyed church of Sant'Agostino in the early nineteenth century — still constitute, in the words of one tradition, the only two surviving funerary monuments of the lords of Padova, the Carraresi, and masterpieces of fourteenth-century sculptural art.

    The most celebrated artistic event in the Eremitani was the decoration of the Ovetari Chapel, a commission that would mark the threshold between the medieval and Renaissance traditions in northern Italy.

    Antonio Ovetari was a Padua notary who, at his death, left a large sum for the decoration of the family chapel in the Eremitani church. The project was carried out by his widow, Imperatrice Ovetari, who in 1448 commissioned the work to a group of artists, which included the elder Giovanni d'Alemagna, Antonio Vivarini (a Venetian late Gothic painter), and two young Paduans, Niccolò Pizzolo and Andrea Mantegna. The latter at the time was seventeen years old and had just begun his apprenticeship in Squarcione's workshop.

    The side walls of the chapel were dedicated to scenes from the lives of Saint James and Saint Christopher, and the apse wall, with its window apertures, was to depict the Assumption of the Virgin. At the end of 1451 the works were halted due to lack of funds. They were restarted in November 1453 and completed in 1457. This second phase saw Mantegna alone at work, as Pizzolo had also died in 1453. Mantegna completed the Stories of Saint James, frescoed the central wall with the Assumption of the Virgin, and completed the lower sector of the Stories of Saint Christopher, where he painted two unified scenes: the Martyrdom of Saint Christopher.

    The frescoes were remarkable for their archaeological precision and startling illusionistic perspective — figures seen from below (di sotto in sù), classical architectural settings, and an almost sculptural treatment of anatomy that was entirely new to the Veneto. Even in the artist's own lifetime, the work attracted controversy: Imperatrice Ovetari accused Mantegna of having painted only eight apostles instead of twelve in the Assumption. Two painters from Milan, Pietro da Milano and Giovanni Storlato, were called in to resolve the matter. They justified Mantegna's choice due to the lack of space.

    The Eremitani attracted figures of European significance across the centuries. Henry III of Valois was received here on his journey toward France to assume the crown (1574). Saint Francis de Sales, when he was a university student in Padova, would come here to pray, from the nearby Via Zabarella where he resided. Martin Luther also stayed at the adjacent convent during his journey to Rome.

    Among those interred within the church are the remains of the cavalier Zanino da Peraga, Ilario Sanguinacci, Jacopo da Forlì, the humanist Marco Mantova Benavides, the noblewoman Vittoria Accoramboni, the physician and biologist Antonio Vallisneri, and the singer and composer Barbara Strozzi.

    The friars were expelled from their house by the Napoleonic Suppression Decree of 28 June 1806. The church was reopened for worship in 1808 and the cloister complex was converted into a military barracks (the Caserma Gattamelata). The adjacent convent — one of the largest in medieval Padova — was ultimately repurposed as the Musei Civici agli Eremitani, which today house halls of archaeological objects and — in the nearby Palazzo Zuckermann — a museum of modern and medieval applied art.

    On the morning of 11 March 1944, the Eremitani was struck by Allied bombs during a raid on Padova. On Saturday 11 March 1944 at 11.45 AM, during the fourth Allied bombing raid on Padova, Mantegna's fresco cycle in the Ovetari Chapel was irreparably destroyed. The raid appears to have been directed at the German command at Arcella, but wind and an imprecise tracking system caused the bomb to fall on the Ovetari Chapel instead. The raid was thus not only a humanitarian disaster, with hundreds of casualties, but also an artistic one.

    The destruction of the church and the shattering of the Ovetari Chapel's famous murals has been called Italy's biggest cultural loss of World War II. The greatest casualty of the bombing was the fresco decoration in the Ovetari Chapel. 88,000 shattered fragments were salvaged and put into storage. But a considerable amount of the fresco was lost forever. Only two scenes had escaped: around 1880 two frescoes — the Assumption and the Martyrdom of Saint Christopher — had been detached from the walls. During World War II these two frescoes were stored in a separate location and were thus saved from the destruction.

    The architect Ferdinando Forlati, responsible for the main restoration work carried out after World War II in the Veneto region, restored the Eremitani church and the Ovetari Chapel. The presbytery of the church had collapsed, as had a portion of the facade. The nave was seriously damaged, and the adornments of the interior were all irreparably lost. The masonry surviving the collapse presented structural offsets ranging from 32 to 50 centimeters. The stage of collecting the debris began immediately in order to recover fragments of Mantegna's frescoes above all. Following the war, the fragments were delivered in 109 cases to the Istituto Centrale del Restauro in Rome, headed at that time by Cesare Brandi.

    In 1946, the thousands of tiny fragments were collected and sent to the Italian Central Institute for Restoration (Istituto Centrale per il Restauro, ICR). Cesare Brandi and Paolo Mora carried out exemplary work restoring one of Mantegna's paintings. However, the scale of the loss made full recovery impossible through traditional means alone.

    The restoration of the Ovetari Chapel began immediately with the recovery of fragments of Mantegna's frescoes. Like a giant jigsaw puzzle, people tried to rebuild that masterpiece — most recently in 2006, when computer technology was used to piece together fragments from 113 cases housing the remains. Computational mathematics, pattern recognition algorithms, and digital imaging were deployed in an unprecedented interdisciplinary effort to reassemble what could be salvaged.

    Today, only two scenes and a few fragments survive, which were restored and repositioned in 2006. They are, however, known from black-and-white photographs that were taken before the war and have become the primary documentary record of one of the most ambitious fresco programs of the early Italian Renaissance.

    The Church of the Eremitani is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Padua's fourteenth-century fresco cycles, inscribed in 2021. This recognition — which encompasses the Scrovegni Chapel, the Palazzo della Ragione, the Baptistery of the Cathedral, and the Oratory of San Giorgio alongside the Eremitani — acknowledges the extraordinary concentration of innovative pictorial programs that made Padova, across the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries, one of the creative centers of European art.

    The Eremitani thus stands as a site of paradox and resilience: a church that once held some of the most luminous painting of the Renaissance, reduced to rubble in a single morning in 1944, and painstakingly rebuilt as a testimony to both irreplaceable loss and the limits and possibilities of modern restoration. For any researcher engaged with the visual and devotional culture of medieval and early Renaissance Italy, it remains an indispensable point of reference — and one directly relevant to the sensory and material questions that scholars such as Zuleika Murat, working just steps away at the University of Padova, continue to investigate today.

F

  1. Fatimid Caliphate (909-1171 CE)

    The Fatimid Caliphate (909-1171 CE) represents one of the most creative and culturally ambitious dynasties in Islamic history. Ruling first from North Africa and then from Egypt, the Fatimids synthesized influences from Abbasid Mesopotamia, Byzantine Constantinople, ancient Egypt, and indigenous North African traditions into a distinctive visual and intellectual culture that exercised influence far beyond the borders of their empire, reaching directly into Norman Sicily and the court of Roger II.

    The Fatimids were an Ismaili Shia dynasty whose founder claimed descent from Fatima, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, and her husband Ali, the first Shia imam. This genealogical claim was not merely dynastic rhetoric but the theological cornerstone of their legitimacy, making the caliph both political sovereign and divinely guided imam. This dual sacred-political authority profoundly shaped Fatimid art and architecture, where ceremonial display functioned as theological performance.

    The dynasty emerged from an Ismaili revolutionary movement in ninth-century Syria and established its first capital at al-Mahdiyya on the Tunisian coast in 921. The conquest of Egypt in 969 inaugurated its greatest phase. The general Jawhar al-Siqilli founded a new capital north of Fustat called al-Qahira ("The Victorious"), modern Cairo. From this imperial seat, the Fatimids presided over one of the most prosperous states in the medieval Mediterranean, drawing wealth from Egypt's agricultural surplus and from control of Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade networks.

    Fatimid religious architecture established a formal vocabulary both innovative and syncretic, combining Abbasid, Byzantine, and North African Berber traditions. Hallmark features include the projected portal, treated as an autonomous element protruding from the facade; the keel-shaped arch with concave sides; and the deliberate alignment of mosque facades with urban streets as decorated public fronts. The dome before the mihrab marked ceremonial authority, while the mihrab and qibla wall received the finest carved stucco and marble programs, where geometric, vegetal, and epigraphic ornament reached exceptional refinement.

    Two key monuments define Fatimid Cairo. Al-Azhar Mosque (969-973), founded with the city itself, became the principal congregational and intellectual center of Fatimid Ismaili learning and remains among the most prestigious institutions of Islamic scholarship. The Mosque of al-Hakim (begun 990, completed 1013) served both devotional and dynastic purposes, with monumental minaret forms and rich carved decoration in stone and stucco that integrated Quranic friezes with geometric and arabesque ornament.

    Three great gates of Cairo's Fatimid walls survive as major works of medieval military architecture: Bab al-Nasr, Bab al-Futuh, and Bab Zuweila, completed under the vizier Badr al-Jamali between 1087 and 1092. Their stone construction and strongly Byzantine-leaning formal language are often linked to Armenian and Syrian Christian craftsmen active in Fatimid service, a revealing sign of the cosmopolitan character of Fatimid state culture.

    Fatimid decorative arts rank among the supreme achievements of medieval Islamic craftsmanship. The royal treasury (khizana) held textiles, rock crystal vessels, ivory carvings, ceramics, metalwork, and jewelry of extraordinary quality. Textiles were especially prestigious, produced in court-sponsored tiraz workshops where inscriptions, dynastic titulature, and elite imagery were woven into silk and linen. The coronation mantle of Roger II in Vienna is regularly cited as a key witness to this Fatimid-influenced textile world as adapted in Norman Sicily.

    Rock crystal carving reached exceptional virtuosity under Fatimid patronage, producing vessels and luxury objects of remarkable thinness and clarity, often decorated with vegetal and animal motifs. Many such works entered European treasuries through diplomacy, trade, and reuse as reliquaries. Fatimid lusterware ceramics circulated widely across the Mediterranean, and in Italy imported bowls (bacini) were embedded into Romanesque church facades and campanili, especially in Tuscany and Liguria, creating one of the most visible forms of cross-Mediterranean artistic exchange.

    Carved woodwork was another signature medium: doors, minbars, screens, and ceiling elements were worked with extraordinary geometric and arabesque depth, and in some contexts with figural motifs. Artistic links with Norman Sicily are particularly strong in this medium; the wooden doors of Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio (La Martorana) in Palermo are associated with craftsmen formed in Fatimid-derived traditions.

    Fatimid manuscript patronage was also significant. The Blue Quran (Qur'an al-Azraq), written in gold and silver Kufic script on indigo-dyed parchment, is one of the most celebrated luxury manuscripts of the medieval Islamic world. Often associated with tenth-century Fatimid Tunisia, it demonstrates dialogue with both North African practices and broader Mediterranean traditions of luxury manuscript production.

    A particularly important aspect of Fatimid visual culture is its substantial figural repertoire in luxury arts, including human and animal imagery in textiles, ivories, ceramics, and courtly painted settings. This distinguishes Fatimid court art from later, more strictly aniconic currents in many Sunni contexts. The painted wooden ceiling of the Cappella Palatina in Palermo, commissioned by Roger II around 1143, remains the largest surviving ensemble of Fatimid-inspired figural painting, preserving in Norman Sicily a visual language deeply indebted to Egypt.

    Intellectually, the Fatimid court developed an elaborate missionary institution, the da'wa ("the call"), organized through a hierarchy of teachers and preachers headed by the da'i al-du'at. Al-Azhar functioned as a major center for doctrinal formation, while the Dar al-Hikmah (House of Wisdom), founded by al-Hakim in 1005, served as library and scholarly institution in law, philosophy, medicine, and the mathematical sciences. These institutions made Cairo one of the leading intellectual capitals of the medieval world.

    The Fatimid Caliphate ended in 1171 when Saladin, vizier to the last Fatimid caliph, dissolved the dynasty and restored Sunni rule in Egypt. Yet Fatimid influence endured: its architectural and ornamental innovations shaped Ayyubid and Mamluk visual culture, while its epigraphic, geometric, and arabesque vocabulary entered the broader language of Mediterranean Islamic and cross-cultural medieval art.

  2. Ferdinando Leopoldo del Migliore

    Ferdinando Leopoldo del Migliore (Florence, 20 August 1628 - Florence, 1696) was an Italian historian, writer, and antiquarian whose work is closely tied to the cultural memory of seventeenth-century Florence. He is best known for compiling an enormous body of archival notes on Florentine history, local families, churches, palaces, and urban traditions, material that later became an important resource for historians of the city.

    Del Migliore was born in Florence to Francesco Migliori and Francesca Vanni. He devoted much of his life to archival research and produced about 120 volumes of excerpts and notes on Florentine history, a vast documentary archive that was eventually transferred to the Biblioteca Magliabechiana and is now preserved in the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Firenze. His activity made him one of the most frequently consulted erudite writers on Florence in the early modern period.

    His first printed work, Senatori fiorentini, appeared in Florence in 1665 and dealt with the families that held the office of senator in the city. In 1684 he published the first volume of Firenze citta nobilissima illustrata, an ambitious survey of Florence that was intended to run to four volumes but remained incomplete because of his sudden death. The book offers a rich panorama of churches, buildings, streets, and families in seventeenth-century Florence.

    Del Migliore's reputation is mixed. Later scholars admired the breadth of his collecting and the value of the information he preserved, especially when original documents were no longer available. At the same time, he was criticized for embellishing archival findings with undocumented details and, in some cases, for inventing documents outright.

    One famous example concerns Salvino degli Armati, the supposed Florentine inventor of eyeglasses; Del Migliore helped promote this attribution by presenting material that later scholars judged unreliable. For this reason, he is remembered both as a valuable local historian and as a problematic source who must be used with caution.

    Despite the doubts surrounding some of his methods, Del Migliore remains an important figure in Florentine historiography because he preserved a large quantity of otherwise inaccessible material. His writings are especially useful for understanding how seventeenth-century Florentines constructed the city's civic memory and noble identity. For researchers of Florence, his work is still significant as a witness to local traditions, even when it must be verified against more secure sources.

  3. Filippo Minutolo

    Filippo Minutolo was born in Naples into the noble Capece Minutolo family, one of the city's most distinguished patrician lineages. He first appears in the documentary record in 1269, when his name is listed, in second position among the deacon-canons, among the signatories of a bull issued by Archbishop Aiglerio of Naples. This early appearance indicates that he had already entered the cathedral chapter as a young cleric of notable rank. Before becoming archbishop, he served as chierico palatino and royal counsellor at the Angevin court, placing him at the center of royal administration.

    His legal and diplomatic skill made him especially valuable to Charles I of Anjou, who entrusted him with several delicate missions. In 1270 he was sent to Tuscany on royal business; on another occasion he traveled to Lombardy to negotiate the liberation of prisoners; and he was dispatched twice to Pisa: first to raise a loan from a Sienese merchant for payment of the papal census, and again in 1272 to settle a commercial and political agreement between the crown and the Commune of Pisa, including the payment of 2,000 gold ounces by the Pisans as satisfaction for earlier offenses. These assignments reveal a figure deeply trusted in matters of high statecraft.

    Filippo was elevated to the archbishopric of Naples in 1288, filling a see that had remained vacant for four years after the death of his French predecessor Aiglerio. His appointment therefore marked both a personal ascent and a renewed Italian presence in one of the kingdom's most important ecclesiastical offices. In the same year he took part in the general Parliament of the Kingdom held at Melfi in August, appearing among the foremost ecclesiastical magnates of Charles II's early reign.

    His moral and intellectual authority at court is vividly attested in a remarkable document of 25 April 1295, in which Charles II, instructing his son Robert on prudent governance, named Filippo Minutolo first among the advisors the prince should consult, praising him as "the venerable father in Christ, Philip Archbishop of Naples." This exceptional endorsement underscores how highly Charles II valued his counsel. Filippo thus functioned as a crucial bridge between the reigns of Charles I and Charles II, and likely influenced the formation of Robert of Anjou, the future Robert "the Wise."

    Filippo Minutolo died on 24 October 1301 and was buried in his family's chapel within the new cathedral of Naples, a space he had already furnished with an altar during his lifetime. His sarcophagus carries a recumbent effigy and a leonine-verse epitaph that summarizes his reputation: "Magnanimus sapiens prudens famaque serenus, / Philippus presul morum dulcedine plenus / Minutulus patrie decus et flos alta propago: hic silet, hic tegitur, iacet hic probitatis imago" ("Magnanimous, wise, prudent, serene in fame, Philip the bishop, full of the sweetness of character, Minutolo, ornament of his homeland and flower of noble lineage: here he is silent, here he is covered, here lies the image of probity").

  4. Florin (Gold Florin of Florence)

    The gold florin was the standard currency of medieval international trade, minted in Florence beginning in 1252 from 24-karat gold, weighing approximately 3.537 grams. It was the most stable and reliable coin in Europe, accepted in major markets from London to Constantinople so much so that historians have often called it "the dollar of the Middle Ages."

    Upon its introduction in 1252, the florin was worth about 20 soldi (1 lira); but during the 13th century, its value in mixed currency gradually increased, reaching around 29 soldi by about 1300, or just under one and a half lire.

    The most telling source for answering this question comes directly from Siena and involves an identical figure. The Spedale di Santa Maria della Scala purchased a precious reliquary, a collection of relics from the imperial treasury, for the sum of 3,000 gold florins, and sources from the time clearly explain what that figure meant: with 3,000 florins, one could build a palace in the center of the city of Siena. The same sources provide a second, equally evocative point of comparison: 3,000 florins were equivalent to the value of a dozen farms.

    To put these figures into further perspective, it is useful to compare them with the wages and costs documented in Siena and Tuscany in the early 14th century. A skilled laborer, a bricklayer or a carpenter, earned about 8-10 soldi a day, or about half a lira a day. Since in 1300 a gold florin was worth about 29 soldi, a skilled worker would need three or four days to earn a single florin. Extending this calculation to 3,000 florins yields a sum equivalent to about 24-25 years' wages for a craftsman working continuously every day of the year, an absolutely enormous amount.

    The ability to move 3,000 florins in a single transaction was therefore the exclusive prerogative of the great Sienese banking families, the Tolomei, the Salimbeni, the Buonsignori, or of institutions such as Santa Maria della Scala itself, which managed assets on an international scale.

  5. Francesco Bossi (Bossio)

    Francesco Bossio, more often written Francesco Bossi in modern scholarship, was a sixteenth-century Milanese jurist and bishop closely associated with Carlo Borromeo and with the institutional implementation of post-Tridentine reform in Italy.

    He was born in Milan in the early sixteenth century to Egidio Bossi, a distinguished jurist and patrician, and Angela de' Pieni. Trained in law, he entered the College of Jurists of Milan and in 1562 edited and published his father's Tractatus varii. As a senator, he delivered a formal oration in 1554 for the accession of Philip (future Philip II) to the Duchy of Milan.

    A decisive turning point came with his Roman period beginning in 1560, when he joined a Milanese delegation sent to congratulate the newly elected Pius IV. During this stay he was appointed consistorial advocate and referendary of the two Signatures. In Rome he formed a lasting relationship with Carlo Borromeo, sustained by correspondence and close collaboration in ecclesiastical reform. He was also influenced by the Sienese spiritual milieu associated with Bonsignore Cacciaguerra and maintained ties with the Barnabites.

    Likely under Borromeo's influence, he moved from legal office into full ecclesiastical service: ordained subdeacon in July 1568, he became bishop of Gravina on 2 August 1568. He had already held major curial and legatine responsibilities, including vice-legations in Perugia and Bologna, and in 1567 he was appointed vicar for Borromeo at Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome.

    On 5 May 1574 he was transferred to Perugia, where he renewed diocesan statutes in the synod of 1575; on 21 October 1579, at Borromeo's request, he was transferred again, this time to Novara, a suffragan see within the Milanese ecclesiastical province. His role in the history of Siena is especially notable: as part of Borromeo's wider program of apostolic visitation, he inspected several dioceses in central and northern Italy, including Siena in 1575, with detailed reports on churches, clergy, confraternities, and devotional life.

    The acts of his apostolic visit to Siena have been critically edited in modern scholarship and are treated as a major source for the religious, artistic, and social history of late sixteenth-century Tuscany. Bossi died in Novara on 18 September 1584. His career exemplifies the post-Tridentine reforming prelate: juristically trained, administratively capable, and closely tied to the Borromean program of disciplined, inspection-based ecclesiastical renewal.

  6. Francis of Assisi

    Francis of Assisi, born Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone in late 1181 or early 1182 in Assisi, was the founder of the Franciscan movement and one of the most transformative religious figures of the High Middle Ages. His life unfolded in a period marked by urban growth, crusading ideology, and intense ecclesiastical reform, and his radical embrace of poverty, humility, and evangelical simplicity offered a direct challenge to the material ambitions of his age.

    He was the son of Pietro di Bernardone, a prosperous cloth merchant whose commercial ties with France helped shape Francis's early taste for troubadour culture, fine textiles, and chivalric ideals. Raised in relative comfort within Assisi's rising merchant class, Francis spent his youth immersed in festivals, sociability, and dreams of knighthood. Around 1202, however, after fighting in the war between Assisi and Perugia, he was captured following the battle of Collestrada and endured more than a year of imprisonment, an experience that, together with subsequent illness, began to unsettle his earlier ambitions.

    After his release, physical weakness and spiritual uncertainty led him toward conversion. A failed journey to Spoleto in 1204 and a sequence of visionary experiences gradually drew him away from his father's business and toward acts of religious repair and charity. By 1205, while praying before the crucifix in the ruined church of San Damiano, he believed he heard Christ command him to "repair my house." At first he interpreted the instruction literally, using money derived from his father's cloth to restore neglected chapels such as San Damiano and Santa Maria degli Angeli (the Porziuncola), a course of action that provoked a decisive break with his family.

    The public turning point came in 1206, when Francis appeared before the bishop of Assisi and renounced his inheritance, symbolically stripping himself of his clothes and placing himself under divine rather than paternal authority. From that moment he embraced radical paupertas, living among lepers, repairing abandoned churches, and cultivating a spirituality grounded in humility, compassion, and identification with society's outcasts. Early Franciscan tradition also associated him with emblematic episodes such as the taming of the wolf of Gubbio, narratives that expressed his vision of creation as a reconciled community under God.

    On 24 February 1208, while attending Mass at the Porziuncola, Francis heard the Gospel passage in which Christ sends the apostles out without money, spare clothing, or worldly security. He took this as the defining rule of his life and began preaching repentance in the vernacular, soon gathering companions such as Bernard of Quintavalle and Peter Catani. By 1209 he had formed the nucleus of the fratres minores, the Friars Minor, and brought an informal rule based on Gospel precepts to Rome. Pope Innocent III, initially cautious, approved the group orally, allowing the Franciscan movement to emerge as a new and powerful model of apostolic life within the Church.

    Francis's influence rapidly extended beyond the first friars. In 1212, Clare of Assisi joined his movement, giving rise to the Poor Clares, while a Third Order developed for lay men and women seeking to live according to Franciscan principles without withdrawing from ordinary society. In this way, Francis helped democratize ideals of sanctity, opening serious religious commitment to a far broader segment of medieval society than older monastic structures had typically allowed.

    His ministry also took on an international and missionary dimension. He attempted voyages connected with the Holy Land and North Africa, and in 1219, during the Fifth Crusade, he crossed to the camp of the Ayyubid sultan al-Malik al-Kamil at Damietta, seeking peaceful witness rather than military triumph. Although no mass conversion resulted, the episode became one of the most celebrated moments in his biography and later Franciscan memory, symbolizing both evangelical boldness and a rare medieval model of interreligious encounter.

    Francis's later years were marked by profound physical suffering and spiritual intensity. At Greccio in 1223 he staged the famous living Nativity, giving enduring form to popular devotion to the Incarnation. In 1224, while in retreat on Mount La Verna, he is said to have received the stigmata, the wounds of Christ impressed upon his own body, making him the first saint in Christian tradition to be so marked. During the same final period of illness he composed the Canticle of the Sun, one of the great vernacular texts of medieval Italy, praising God through "Brother Sun," "Sister Moon," and the whole created order.

    Francis died on 3 October 1226 at the Porziuncola and was canonized with extraordinary speed on 16 July 1228 by Pope Gregory IX. The basilica built over his tomb at Assisi quickly became one of the major artistic and devotional centers of medieval Europe, and his life inspired an immense textual and visual tradition, from Thomas of Celano and Bonaventure to the fresco cycles later associated with Cimabue and Giotto. His legacy transformed medieval Christianity by making poverty, compassion, imitation of Christ, and reverence for creation central to religious imagination, and his influence has continued far beyond the Middle Ages in theology, literature, art, and modern ecological thought.

  7. Frater Elia of Cortona

    Frater Elia of Cortona was one of the most important and controversial figures in the early Franciscan movement: a close associate of St. Francis, an able organizer, builder, and leader, but also a man later criticized for his style of government and his political choices. He was born near Assisi around 1170–1180, died in Cortona on 22 April 1253, and became a central actor in shaping the institutional Franciscan Order.

    The sources are uncertain about Elia's earliest years, but the best biographical tradition places his birth near Assisi and gives him the name Buonbarone, or Bonusbaro. Treccani notes that later sources are sparse and sometimes biased, yet they suggest he may have worked as a schoolmaster, a mattress-maker, or even a notary in Bologna before joining Francis's movement. His rise is striking because he entered the friars relatively late, likely between 1210 and 1215, after which he quickly became one of Francis's most trusted companions.

    Elia's importance grew rapidly when Francis sent him in 1217 to the Holy Land as minister provincial of Syria. He returned with Francis in 1220 and was named vicar of the Order in 1221, which made him the practical administrator of the friars during Francis's final years. Treccani emphasizes that Francis entrusted him with enforcing the Rule and managing the order's expansion, while contemporary and near-contemporary sources present him as a faithful interpreter of Francis's will.

    After Francis's death in 1226, Elia played a decisive role in announcing the saint's passing and in promoting the public cult of the stigmata. He then became the driving force behind the Basilica of Saint Francis in Assisi, securing the land, organizing funding, and overseeing construction. Later tradition even credited him with architectural planning for the basilica's two-tiered design, though that attribution is not certain. In historical terms, his greatest lasting achievement was to give the Franciscan memory a monumental architectural form.

    Elia was elected minister general in 1232, but his leadership became increasingly contested. Critics accused him of authoritarian methods, luxury, and insufficient respect for Franciscan poverty, while supporters saw him as a strong administrator needed to govern a fast-growing order. His political alignment with Frederick II deepened the conflict, and he was deposed in 1239; he was then excommunicated in 1240 and again in 1244. After these ruptures, he withdrew to Cortona, where his life became bound up with local patronage and with the church of San Francesco he helped build there.

    Elia's final years were spent in or around Cortona, and he died there on 22 April 1253. Treccani indicates that he was eventually reconciled with the Church before death, a detail that matters because later Franciscan tradition often turned him into a symbol of corruption and apostasy. That negative image became powerful in later medieval narratives, but modern scholarship tends to see a more nuanced figure: a brilliant organizer, a builder of institutions, and a controversial reformer caught between Francis's ideal of poverty and the demands of a rapidly expanding order.

    His biography is therefore not only the story of a friar, but also a window into the early transformation of the Franciscan movement from a charismatic brotherhood into a structured religious institution.

  8. Frederick Barbarossa (Frederick I, Holy Roman Emperor)

    Frederick I of Swabia, known as Barbarossa - a nickname given to him by the towns of northern Italy because of his thick, reddish beard - was Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire from 1155 until his death in 1190, and remains one of the most powerful, ambitious, and controversial medieval rulers in all of European history. His reign of nearly forty years was marked by six military expeditions to Italy, a long and bitter conflict with the papacy, and a proud vision of restoring the full translatio imperii of ancient Rome.

    Frederick was born around 1122, the son of Frederick II, Duke of Swabia, of the House of Hohenstaufen, and Judith of Bavaria, of the House of Welf. This dual lineage - from two of the most powerful and rival families of medieval Germany - placed him in a unique position to mediate between the Guelph and Ghibelline factions that were tearing the German realm apart. When Emperor Conrad III died in 1152 without leaving a direct successor capable of garnering broad support, the German princes elected Frederick King of Germany on March 4 in Frankfurt, and crowned him in Aachen on March 9 of the same year. It was a choice dictated by the need to mend the rift between the Guelphs and Ghibellines, relying on a young man who represented both houses by blood.

    In 1154-1155, Frederick traveled to Italy for the first time, with the aim of asserting his imperial authority over a politically turbulent peninsula, reestablishing control over the rebellious cities, and obtaining the imperial crown from the pope.

    In Pavia, he received the crown of King of Italy, then destroyed the city of Tortona, an ally of Milan, and on June 18, 1155, he was crowned emperor by Pope Adrian IV in Rome - the same pope who, a few months earlier, had chosen his disciple Eugene III, a Cistercian from Pisa, as his own advisor. Returning to Germany almost immediately, Frederick had resolved nothing: in 1158 he descended again with a far larger army and, at the Diet of Roncaglia, promulgated the Constitutiones, a body of imperial laws that claimed rights for the crown over all the cities of Italy, including the collection of duties and taxes that the communes had by then come to regard as their own.

    The response from the communes of northern Italy was swift and organized: in 1167, while Frederick was marching toward Rome with a large army - capturing the city on July 24 and installing an antipope, Paschal III, in exchange for a new imperial coronation - sixteen northern cities signed the Lombard League, with Milan at the helm, to collectively defend their autonomy. A terrible malaria epidemic decimated the imperial army near Rome in the summer of 1167, forcing Frederick into a hasty retreat: a sudden reversal that many contemporaries interpreted as divine punishment. The decisive confrontation came on May 29, 1176, at Legnano, in Lombardy, where the infantry of the communes - supported by the famous Milanese Carroccio - routed the German cavalry: it was a defeat that deeply shook the emperor's myth of invincibility.

    Parallel to the Italian wars, Frederick waged a long conflict with the papacy that lasted nearly twenty years. In 1159, upon the death of Pope Adrian IV, a double election divided Christendom: Frederick supported the antipope Victor IV against the canonically elected Alexander III, creating a schism that was resolved only in 1177 with the Treaty of Venice. In that agreement, Frederick recognized Alexander III as the legitimate pope, formally renouncing his claims to supremacy over papal appointments, and in return secured the restoration of peace with the Italian communes, which was then definitively ratified by the Peace of Constance in 1183. The Peace of Constance was his most significant political concession: he recognized the Lombard communes' right to self-govern in civil matters, to maintain armies, and to form alliances, retaining only formal obedience to the emperor.

    While Barbarossa suffered numerous setbacks in Italy, his rule in Germany was more stable and constructive. He reorganized the German feudal system, promoting expansion eastward into Slavic territories - the Drang nach Osten - and encouraging trade and urban development.

    His most dangerous internal antagonist was Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, a powerful Guelph prince who had refused to participate in the Italian campaign of 1176, thereby indirectly contributing to the defeat at Legnano. In 1180 Frederick banished Henry the Lion from the Empire, confiscated his duchies, and exiled him to England, redistributing his lands to loyal princes: this was a consolidation of imperial power on the German front that partially offset the losses in Italy.

    In the summer of 1189, Frederick set out on the Third Crusade at the age of sixty-six, at the head of one of the largest armies ever assembled in the West, with forces estimated at between 100,000 and 150,000 men.

    The expedition crossed the Balkans and Anatolia amid enormous logistical difficulties, but Frederick kept the army cohesive and on the move. On June 10, 1190, he attempted to cross the Saleph River - today's Goksu, in southern Turkey - perhaps to shorten the route or to water his horse, and drowned in the river's cold, swirling waters. His sudden death was a shock to the crusade: most of the army scattered, and only a small portion continued on toward the Holy Land.

    The figure of Barbarossa immediately transcended history to become a legend. Beginning in the 13th century, a tradition spread in Germany that the emperor had not died but was sleeping beneath Mount Kyffhauser in Thuringia, waiting to awaken when Germany needed him to usher in an era of justice and greatness. This medieval myth was revived for propaganda purposes in the modern era: the Wilhelmine emperor inaugurated the great Kyffhauser monument in 1896, and the name "Operation Barbarossa" was given in 1941 to the German invasion of the Soviet Union, symbolically appropriating the image of the medieval conqueror.

  9. Froilan of Leon (San Froilan)

    Froilan of Leon, known in Spanish as San Froilan, was one of the most consequential ecclesiastical figures of ninth-century Iberia: a hermit turned itinerant preacher, a founder of major monasteries, a close collaborator of the Astur-Leonese crown in the repopulation of the Reconquista frontier, and ultimately the Bishop of Leon from 900 until his death in 905. He is venerated as the patron saint of both Leon and Lugo, and his feast day is celebrated on 3 October (with his traditional death date held to be 5 October). His relics are enshrined in the Cathedral of Leon.

    Froilan was born in the province of Lugo in 833, where he began his religious training in one of the most ancient episcopal cities of the Iberian Peninsula, founded by the Romans and surrounded by walls that still stand today. His hagiographic tradition emphasizes that after studying until the age of eighteen, he decided to abandon his studies and become a hermit, seeking the freedom to pray and deepen his relationship with God.

    He retired first to the Gruta de Ruiterlan in the El Bierzo region, today preserved as a hermitage, and later withdrew to the Leonese mountains of Curueno. The Bierzo valley, nestled between the mountains of Galicia and the Leonese meseta, had long been a terrain of ascetic retreat; Froilan took his place in a tradition of Hispanic monasticism rooted in the earlier practices of figures such as Martin of Braga and the desert fathers whose spirituality had been transmitted through the Visigothic and Mozarabic church.

    The pivotal moment in Froilan's biography is described in hagiographic sources through a striking miracle. Seeking a divine sign as to whether he should abandon his contemplative life, Froilan placed burning coals in his mouth and suffered no harm. He interpreted this as a call, a fire of divine love he was now charged to carry to others, and he subsequently traveled through numerous towns in Lugo, Leon, Zamora, Asturias, and Cantabria as a gifted speaker and preacher, converting many to Christianity.

    This combination of extreme asceticism with a missionary drive places Froilan within a broader pattern of early medieval Iberian holy men who moved fluidly between solitude and apostolate, a pattern paralleling, in the western Iberian context, the peregrini ideal of Irish monasticism that had also deeply influenced the Visigothic church.

    During one of his evangelizing journeys, Froilan encountered Atilano, the future Saint Atilano and Bishop of Zamora, with whom he formed a profound and lasting friendship. The two became inseparable companions, combining the eremitic and the coenobitic vocations in a characteristic pattern of ninth-century Iberian monasticism. Together they withdrew to the mountains of Curueno in Leon, but the people followed Froilan to his solitary cell in great numbers, including magnates and bishops eager to hear him preach.

    Pressed by their persistent appeals, he descended to the city of Veseo, where he built his first monastery, which quickly filled with three hundred monks, marking the beginning of his new vocation as a founder of monasteries. Froilan served as abbot; Atilano as prior.

    Froilan's fame crossed the mountains of Leon and reached the court of Alfonso III in Oviedo. The king sent messengers summoning him to court, and was profoundly impressed by the monk. Alfonso III (el Magno, 848-910), the most formidable of the Asturian monarchs, had inherited from his father Ordono I an ambitious programme of territorial expansion and repopulation southward along the valley of the Duero. Monasteries were integral instruments of this policy: they served as centers of settlement, spiritual authority, agricultural organization, and cultural production in territories recently wrested from or exposed to Muslim raiding.

    Alfonso III, amazed by the two saints, granted them broad powers and undertook to fund the construction of several monasteries along the banks of the Duero, for which Froilan and Atilano would be responsible.

    The two foundations that resulted from this royal commission were among the most important religious establishments of their age.

    San Salvador de Tabara (near Zamora) was a double monastery, housing both monks and nuns in separate but adjacent communities, a model with deep roots in the Visigothic tradition. According to the deacon Juan, Froilan "built the monastery of Tabara, where he gathered six hundred servants of God, of both sexes." Froilan served as abbot and Atilano as prior; the illuminator Magio (Magius) made the Tabara scriptorium famous.

    Moreruela was the second foundation, built near the river Esla "in a pleasant and high place," where Froilan gathered another two hundred monks. This monastery would later, in the twelfth century, become one of the earliest Cistercian foundations in Spain, its Benedictine heritage directly linked to Froilan's original endowment.

    Of particular significance to the history of medieval manuscript culture is the scriptorium of San Salvador de Tabara, which Froilan's monastic foundation brought into being. The tower scriptorium of the San Salvador de Tabara Monastery was one of the most important sites for manuscript production during the tenth and eleventh centuries.

    The scriptorium's most celebrated product is the Beatus of Tabara (completed 970), a copy of the Commentary on the Apocalypse by Beatus of Liebana. The manuscript was completed by the scribe Emeterius on 29 July 970; its illumination was begun by the monk Magius, who may be the same master as the "Maius" who illuminated the Morgan Beatus, but who died before completing the Tabara manuscript.

    The Tabara Codex is remarkable above all for its extensive colophon and its depiction of the monastic scriptorium, which preserves the oldest surviving image of a scriptorium in European art. The miniature shows the tower of the monastery with scribes at work, a priceless visual document of the material and intellectual life of a monastic house that Froilan himself had established. This miniature of the tower alta et lapidea contains two scriveners working in the scriptorium and, in an adjacent room, a figure cutting the skin of an animal, that is, preparing parchment.

    The Tabara scriptorium is also associated with the transmission of the Gerona Beatus (c. 975), illuminated in part by Ende, regarded as the first documented female artist in medieval Europe, who spent time at the Tabara monastery and may have belonged to the community of dominae who lived in the double monastery's female precinct.

    When Bishop Vicente of Leon died in 900, the people asked King Alfonso III to appoint Froilan as the new bishop, while Atilano was named Bishop of Zamora. Both men were consecrated on the same day, the feast of Pentecost, 19 May 900, and the king and his entire court attended the ceremonies, which gives a sense of the political and spiritual importance attributed to these appointments.

    Froilan's reluctance to accept the episcopate is a recurring theme in his hagiographic tradition, consistent with the Benedictine and ascetic ideal of humility before ecclesiastical office, a topos with deep roots in patristic literature, from the Life of Martin of Tours onward. One source notes that Froilan had no formal training as a priest, and that Alfonso III was obliged to persuade the reluctant monk to accept the bishopric.

    As bishop, Froilan continued to lead a simple life and showed great love for the poor, even as he held the most prestigious see in the kingdom. He also maintained the prophetic gifts for which he had long been known: in his final years he urged the king, the clergy, and the people to seek through prayer the help and mercy of the Lord, and he is said to have predicted the day and hour of his death.

    Froilan died in Leon on 5 October 905 and was buried in the cathedral, or the old church of Santa Maria, in a magnificent tomb that Alfonso III had built for himself but gave to his beloved bishop. The contemporary chronicles record that "the devout inhabitants of Leon wept bitterly at the loss of their holy shepherd Froilan."

    The subsequent history of his relics is itself a document of medieval devotional politics. His remains were translated in 916 by order of King Ordono II to the new cathedral. When the hajib Almanzor sacked Leon (990-992), the relics were moved to the church of San Juan de Valdecesar, and from there to the Cistercian monastery of Moreruela, the house Froilan himself had founded. This provoked a bitter dispute between the monks of Moreruela and the people and ecclesiastical representatives of Leon, both of whom claimed the saint's body; the pope eventually resolved the conflict by ordering the relics to be divided equitably.

    Froilan was canonized by Pope Urban II (pontificate 1088-1099) and was included in the Roman Martyrology in 1724.

    Froilan is most commonly depicted in the company of a wolf, owing to the tradition that on one of his pilgrimages a hungry wolf attacked and killed his donkey. Yet the wolf was tamed by the saint's kind gaze and words of peace. The legend continues that the wolf thereafter carried the saint's baggage in place of the slain animal, a motif rooted in the widespread hagiographic topos of the holy man's authority over wild nature, most famously associated with Francis of Assisi three centuries later. In the iconographic tradition, Froilan appears as a bearded bishop or monk, typically with a wolf at his feet or beside him, sometimes carrying the episcopal cross or a model of one of his monasteries.

    Froilan of Leon stands at the intersection of several of the most vital forces in ninth-century Iberian history: the tension between eremitic and communal forms of monasticism; the royal instrumentalization of religious foundations as tools of the Reconquista; the survival and renewal of Visigothic and Mozarabic ecclesiastical culture under Christian rule; and the emergence of Leon as the spiritual and political capital of the Christian north. His monastic foundations along the Duero frontier, particularly Tabara, with its celebrated scriptorium, represent enduring contributions to the material culture of the early medieval Iberian Church, whose fruits in illuminated manuscript production would be felt for generations after his death.

G

  1. Ghibellines

    The Ghibellines were the pro-imperial faction in medieval Italy, opposing the pro-papal Guelphs, and their history runs from the late 11th century through the 14th and into the early Renaissance. Their identity evolved from a dynastic struggle in Germany into a complex web of local power conflicts inside Italian city-states, shaping the politics, art, and social life of regions such as Tuscany and Lombardy.

    The labels "Guelph" and "Ghibelline" derive from the rivalry between two German noble houses: the Welfs (Guelfs) and the Hohenstaufen-linked Waiblingen (hence Ghibellino). As the German princes contested the title of Holy Roman Emperor in the 12th century, those who supported the Hohenstaufen rulers, especially Frederick I Barbarossa, came to be known in Italy as Ghibellines, while supporters of the Welf-aligned papal party were called Guelphs.

    This split became politically meaningful in Italy when Frederick Barbarossa sought to reassert direct imperial control over the prosperous Lombard cities, which fiercely defended their autonomy. The Lombard League, backed by the pope, coalesced as a Guelph-leaning alliance, while urban elites who stood to gain from imperial charters, titles, or military backing gravitated toward Ghibellinism.

    The party's most coherent "imperial" phase came under Frederick II (crowned emperor in 1220), who ruled from Sicily and sought to dominate central and northern Italy against successive popes. Within many cities, Ghibelline factions typically included feudal-minded nobles, bishops loyal to the emperor, and some merchant elites who saw imperial overlordship as a way to curb the power of local aristocratic Guelph clans.

    In Florence, for example, Ghibelline governments in the 1240s tried to broaden their base by including the popolo (merchant guilds and artisans), introducing mixed institutions such as the primo popolo and shared captaincies. These experiments show that Ghibellinism was not simply "aristocratic" nor always anti-urban; rather, it was a shifting coalition of interests anchored ultimately in loyalty to the emperor.

    By the mid-13th century, the Guelph-Ghibelline divide became less about the empire versus the papacy and more about internal urban power struggles. In Florence, Bologna, Siena, and other communes, control of the city government often shifted from one faction to the other after armed clashes or sieges, usually ending with the exile of the losing party and the confiscation or destruction of their towers and palaces.

    In Florence, the Ghibellines enjoyed periods of dominance in the 1240s and again after their victory at the Battle of Montaperti in 1260, when Sienese-led Ghibelline forces routed the Florentine Guelph army. Such victories often led to campaigns of architectural demolition, as Ghibelline mobs pulled down Guelph towers, leaving a permanent mark on the urban landscape that can still be traced in the ruined or truncated tower-houses of Tuscany.

    The death of Frederick II in 1250 and the eventual defeat and execution of his grandson Conradin at the Battle of Tagliacozzo (1268) shattered the Hohenstaufen line and with it the core imperial project that Ghibellinism had embodied. After Conradin's public beheading, the Guelph-backed Charles of Anjou became king of Sicily, consolidating papal and French power in southern Italy and weakening remaining Ghibelline strongholds.

    In the decades that followed, Ghibelline networks persisted mainly as local aristocratic or regional groupings rather than as a coherent imperial party. Some cities, such as Forli in Romagna, remained Ghibelline bastions, while elsewhere Guelph dominance hardened, especially in Florence where the Ghibellines were largely expelled or forced underground after the 1266 victory of Charles of Anjou.

    Even after the Hohenstaufens' fall, the Guelph-Ghibelline split did not vanish overnight. In the 14th century, the terms continued to mark coalitions in the Italian wars, such as the clashes between Bologna (Guelph) and Modena (Ghibelline) over the famous "War of the Bucket," and the favor that some Ghibelline families showed to Emperor Louis IV's invasion of Italy. In the 15th and 16th centuries, noble houses such as the Colonna or Gonzaga could still be described as Ghibellines, meaning they reliably backed the Holy Roman Emperor, while others (like the Orsini) remained aligned with French or papal interests.

    Culturally, the Guelph-Ghibelline divide shaped literary and political thought: Dante, himself a Guelph driven into exile, treated the conflict as a central backdrop for his reflection on justice, factionalism, and the failure of the universal empire in the Vita Nuova and De Monarchia. Across Italian museums and churches, this history appears encoded in fresco cycles, inscriptions, and civic monuments, where the choice of imperial or papal imagery often signals the former allegiance of the patrons who commissioned them.

  2. Ghirlandina (Civic Bell Tower of Modena)

    The Ghirlandina is the civic bell tower of Modena Cathedral and one of the defining monuments of the city's medieval identity. Its history is inseparable from that of the Duomo: construction began in the early twelfth century as part of the wider cathedral complex initiated in 1099, but the tower was built in successive campaigns over more than two centuries. This long chronology explains its layered character, where an essentially Romanesque structural core was gradually completed with later additions shaped by changing technical needs and ceremonial functions.

    The lower stages belong to the same building culture associated with Lanfranco's cathedral workshop, with Lombard-Romanesque masonry rhythms, narrow openings in the lower levels, and progressive lightening upward through biforas and triforas. In the later twelfth and thirteenth centuries, Campionese masters were central to the continuation of the work, coordinating structural completion with the broader reorganization of the cathedral's southern front toward Piazza Grande. The tower was not an isolated campanile: it functioned as part of a civic-sacred ensemble linking episcopal authority, communal institutions, and urban ceremonial space.

    Its most recognizable upper termination, the octagonal lantern and crowning zone, was completed in 1319, traditionally associated with Arrigo (Enrico) da Campione and later Campionese activity. By that stage, the tower had become both bell tower and communal symbol, used for liturgical peals, civic alarms, and public signaling. The name "Ghirlandina" is generally connected to the decorative railings or "ghirlande" near the summit, and by the late Middle Ages the tower had already acquired a distinct urban identity beyond its strictly ecclesiastical role.

    In modern historiography the Ghirlandina is read as a rare case of long-duration medieval construction that still preserves a strong formal unity despite multiple phases. Together with the cathedral and Piazza Grande, it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, recognized as an exceptional testimony to the civic and religious culture of the Romanesque city in northern Italy.

  3. Giacomo (Jacopo) Colonna

    Giacomo (or Jacopo) Colonna was one of the most prominent and controversial Roman prelates of the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries, embodying both the political weight of the Colonna family and the turbulent conflicts between Papacy and Roman baronage under Boniface VIII. Born around 1250 and dying in Avignon on 14 August 1318, his life spanned the height of Colonna influence in the College of Cardinals and the dramatic relocation of the papal court to France.

    Giacomo belonged to the senior branch of the Colonna-of-Palestrina line, sons of Oddone of Giordano and Margherita Orsini, a connection that placed him at the heart of Roman aristocratic politics. As a younger scion of a powerful and historically Ghibelline-leaning baronial house, he was directed toward an ecclesiastical career; sources indicate he studied in Bologna, likely in law or theology, which was typical for high-ranking Roman nobles destined for church office. Little survives on his formative years, but chronicles such as those of Salimbene da Parma hint at his early presence in papal circles, where he appeared as a figure capable of negotiating spiritual privileges and local indulgences.

    On 12 March 1278, his first cousin Pope Nicholas III elevated Giacomo to the cardinalate as cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata, a move widely interpreted as reinforcing the Colonna family's preeminence within the Roman Curia. This appointment coincided with Nicholas III's broader strategy of entrusting key Roman families with leadership roles, and Giacomo soon figured as a legatee and executor in testamentary affairs of other senior cardinals, such as Giacomo Savelli (later Pope Honorius IV), underscoring his standing among the Roman baron-clergy. By 1288, he also became arciprete (archpriest) of the Basilica Liberiana (Santa Maria Maggiore), a prestigious liturgical and administrative role that gave him responsibility over one of Rome's four major basilicas.

    In his capacity as arciprete of Santa Maria Maggiore, Giacomo played a central role in the late-thirteenth-century restoration and decoration of the Liberian basilica, in collaboration with Pope Nicholas IV. Together with the pope, he initiated building and mosaic projects in the basilica, including the commission of the renowned mosaicist Giacomo Torriti, whose work in the apse and nave helped define the late-Roman-Byzantine style that became typical of the basilica in that period. These works not only enhanced the sacred prestige of a major pilgrimage site but also served as a visible monument to Colonna influence in the Roman Church, blending devotional display with dynastic self-promotion.

    Tensions erupted during the conclave of 1294, when Giacomo and his nephew Pietro Colonna opposed the election of Benedetto Caetani as Pope Boniface VIII, issuing the so-called manifesto of Lunghezza that questioned the validity of Pope Celestine V's resignation and thus the legitimacy of Boniface's election. The dispute intensified in 1297 when Giacomo, embroiled in a family quarrel with his brothers Ottone, Matteo, and Landolfo, dispossessed them of their lands; the brothers appealed to Boniface, who ordered Giacomo to restore their holdings and surrender the family's castles, including Colonna and Palestrina, to the Papacy. Giacomo refused, triggering a dramatic escalation: in May 1297 Boniface formally deposed him from the College of Cardinals, stripped him of his offices, and excommunicated him and his supporters.

    Deprived of his title and sacraments, Giacomo joined his kinsmen in armed resistance against Boniface VIII, an episode that contributed to the broader crisis culminating in the alleged "outrage of Anagni" and the pope's death in 1303. After Boniface's death, the newly elected Pope Benedict XI withdrew the excommunications imposed on Giacomo and Pietro, yet they were excluded from the 1304 conclave due to the lingering canonical cloud. Full rehabilitation came only under Pope Clement V, who on 17 December 1305 formally reinstated Giacomo as cardinal and restored his arcipresbyterate of Santa Maria Maggiore, later naming him cardinal protodiacono and granting him the title church of San Lorenzo in Lucina.

    During the Avignon period Giacomo appears as a figure working to repair the Colonna reputation and consolidate their ecclesiastical holdings, while still retaining considerable authority in Roman affairs. He remained closely involved in Roman projects, including organizing the rebuilding of the Lateran basilica after the devastating fire of May 1308, underscoring his role as a key administrator for the damaged papal complex in the Eternal City. He also participated in several conclaves, including those of 1280-81 (election of Martin IV), 1287-88 (Nicholas IV), 1292-94 (Celestine V), 1294 (Boniface VIII), and the long conclave of 1314-16 that produced Pope John XXII.

    Giacomo Colonna died in Avignon on 14 August 1318, most likely in the context of the papal court's continued residence in southern France. His remains were later translated to Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome, where his tomb in the Liberian basilica became a focal point for the Colonna family's ecclesiastical memory. Historiographically, he is remembered both as a representative of the powerful Roman baron-cardinals whose rivalry with the papacy contributed to the "Babylonian Captivity" on the Rhone, and as a significant patron of late-thirteenth-century Roman art whose interventions helped shape the visual theology of Santa Maria Maggiore and, indirectly, the aesthetics of later Roman mosaics.

  4. Gionata, Archbishop of Otranto

    Archbishop Gionata of Otranto was the Latin archbishop of Otranto in the second half of the 12th century, and the most secure date associated with his episcopate is the commissioning of the great cathedral mosaic in 1163. He is remembered less for a surviving documentary career than for this major patronage, which made him an important figure in the artistic and ecclesiastical history of Apulia. Gionata governed Otranto at a time when the city was fully integrated into the cultural world of Norman southern Italy, where Latin, Byzantine, and local traditions coexisted. His name is chiefly associated with the famous floor mosaic in Otranto Cathedral, often called the Tree of Life mosaic. According to the available sources, the work was commissioned in 1163 under Gionata's authority and executed by the monk Pantaleone with a mixed team of craftsmen; this makes Gionata the patron of one of the most extraordinary medieval church pavements in Europe.
