    Because the Lira relied on self-declaration, it was vulnerable to underassessment by wealthier taxpayers. To address this problem, the Sienese government of the Nine ordered between 1315 and 1316 a more objective general cadastral survey of immovable property. Conducted between 1316 and 1320, this produced the celebrated Tavola delle Possessioni, often considered the earliest surviving serial cadastral documentation in Europe. The Tavola did not replace the Lira, but functioned alongside it as a cadastral reference, while Siena continued to rely on the older systems of Lira and Preste for ordinary fiscal administration.

  4. Liutprand, King of the Lombards

    Liutprand was king of the Lombards from 712 to 744, marking one of the longest and most transformative reigns in the kingdom's history on the Italian peninsula. Born around 680, he ascended the throne amid familial tragedy — his father Ansprand had been exiled by rivals, his brother blinded, and his mother and sister mutilated — yet he swiftly consolidated power after overthrowing King Aripert II, ruling for 31 years with a blend of military prowess, diplomatic acumen, and legislative innovation. His rule began aggressively, targeting Byzantine territories in Italy such as Ravenna's exarchate; he captured key sites like Bologna, Osimo, Rimini, Ancona, and the port of Classe, while maintaining a strategic alliance with the Franks under Charles Martel, cemented by his marriage to Guntrud, daughter of Bavarian duke Theodo I. Liutprand stands out for his extensive law-giving, issuing edicts in fifteen separate sessions between 713 and 735, which modernized Lombard law beyond tribal customs toward a more centralized royal authority; this legal corpus, preserved in the Edictum Langobardorum, not only stabilized his realm but left a lasting administrative legacy. A pivotal moment came in 728 with the Donation of Sutri, where Liutprand symbolically ceded the town near Rome to Pope Gregory II after initial seizures — the first grant of sovereign territory to the papacy. Tensions resurfaced under Pope Gregory III, but Liutprand signed a 20-year truce with Zachary in 741, prioritizing stability over conquest in his later years. Liutprand died in 744 in Pavia and was buried in the Basilica of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro. Historians regard him as the most effective Lombard king, achieving hegemonic influence across Italy through conquests, legal reforms, and balanced foreign policy.

  5. Louis of Toulouse (Louis of Anjou)

    Louis of Toulouse, also known as Louis of Anjou, was a Neapolitan prince of the Capetian House of Anjou who renounced his rights to a royal throne in order to become a Franciscan friar and bishop, and was canonized as a saint in 1317. His brief life, marked by captivity, radical poverty and early episcopal office, made him a paradigmatic figure of Angevin piety and Franciscan spirituality at the turn of the fourteenth century.

    Louis was born on 9 February 1274, probably at Brignoles in Provence, then part of the territories ruled by his Angevin family. He was the second son of Charles II of Anjou, later king of Naples and Sicily, and Mary (or Maria) of Hungary, placing him at the intersection of Capetian French and Hungarian royal lineages. Through his father he was a great-nephew of King Saint Louis IX of France, while on his mother's side he was related to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary and Saint Margaret of Hungary, giving him what contemporaries saw as an "impeccable saintly lineage." The family's dominions encompassed Provence, the kingdom of Naples and claims over Sicily and Jerusalem, and Louis grew up in a milieu shaped by dynastic warfare and crusading ambitions.

    From an early age Louis was described as unusually devout and charitable, reportedly taking food from the castle to distribute to the poor and showing a particular concern for the sick. Later Franciscan hagiography emphasized his attraction to prayer and to the corporal works of mercy, building an image of a prince whose spiritual disposition anticipated his eventual renunciation of worldly power.

    The decisive formative experience of Louis's youth came when he was taken hostage in the context of the War of the Sicilian Vespers, the violent conflict over Angevin control of southern Italy. Around the age of fourteen, Louis and two of his brothers were handed over as hostages to the Aragonese court as part of a political settlement involving their father Charles II and the king of Aragon. The brothers spent approximately seven years in captivity in Catalonia, probably in or near Barcelona, where they lived under relatively honorable conditions but remained pawns in Mediterranean power politics.

    During this period the Angevin princes were educated by Franciscan friars, whose teaching combined scholastic formation with an emphasis on evangelical poverty and care for the marginalized. Under their influence Louis deepened his spiritual life, developed a special love for the poor and for those afflicted by leprosy, and gradually formed the intention to renounce his royal status in order to become a Franciscan. Sources record that while still a hostage he resolved internally to abandon the succession and embrace a life patterned on that of Saint Francis of Assisi.

    Louis's spiritual project was complicated by a change in dynastic circumstances. His elder brother Charles Martel, originally heir to the Angevin claims, died unexpectedly, which placed Louis next in line to inherit the throne of Naples and the associated titles, including the largely nominal claim to the kingdom of Jerusalem. This made him, in theory, a future ruler whose decisions would shape the balance of power in the central Mediterranean, and family and papal interests pressed him toward acceptance of his political destiny.

    Upon his release from captivity in 1295, Louis acted dramatically on his long-nurtured intention to abandon worldly power. He formally renounced his rights of succession in favor of his younger brother Robert, who would later rule as Robert of Anjou, king of Naples, thereby diverting the dynastic line and strengthening his brother's legitimacy with the aura of his own sanctity. Hagiographical tradition reports him saying that "Jesus Christ is my kingdom" and that Christ alone was his true wealth, phrases that encapsulate the Franciscan ideal of spiritual lordship through poverty. This renunciation had major political repercussions but also underpinned the later cult, in which Louis appeared as a prince who chose the mendicant life over a crown.

    Louis's desire was to become an ordinary friar, but his royal birth made this impossible in the eyes of the papacy and his family. Pope Boniface VIII and Angevin advisers sought to harness his sanctity and his lineage for ecclesiastical politics, and in 1296 he was designated to the bishopric of Toulouse, a strategically important see in southern France. In order to reconcile his vocation with this appointment, the pope allowed him to make his Franciscan profession first, so that he entered the Order of Friars Minor and then, only a few days later, was ordained priest and consecrated bishop.

    Some sources mention that he had first been proposed for the archbishopric of Lyon around 1295, an appointment he either refused or which did not come to fruition, suggesting that both court and papacy were searching for an appropriate episcopal role that would not overly inflame political tensions. On 5 February 1297 he was consecrated bishop of Toulouse, at a very young age and with limited experience, embodying the intertwining of noble birth and ecclesiastical office characteristic of the late thirteenth century.

    Despite the brevity of his tenure, Louis acquired a reputation for notable pastoral zeal and generosity in Toulouse. He reportedly adopted a simple lifestyle consonant with the Franciscan rule, even while bound to the ceremonial and administrative obligations of a great bishopric. Contemporary and later accounts emphasize that he allocated a large portion-often said to be half to three-quarters-of the episcopal revenues to the poor and to the maintenance of churches, and that he daily fed a group of the indigent at his own table. These stories, though shaped by hagiographic convention, point to a deliberate effort to translate mendicant ideals into the context of high ecclesiastical office.

    Louis is also portrayed as devoutly attentive to liturgical duties and visitation of his diocese, though his health appears to have been fragile and his period in office extremely short, lasting only a few months. His attachment to the Franciscan spirit remained strong: he continued to describe Christ as his only riches and sought to live as closely as possible to the friars' poverty, even while carrying a crozier and wearing a mitre.

    Louis soon came to believe that he could not, or should not, continue as bishop of Toulouse and sought to resign the see in order to live more fully his Franciscan vocation. After only about six months in office he left his diocese and set out for Italy, intending to present his resignation personally to the pope, which suggests both a sense of responsibility and the hierarchical constraints under which he operated. On the journey, however, he fell ill, probably with a fever that some sources identify as typhoid, and died on 19 August 1297 at Brignoles, the place of his birth.

    He was only twenty-three years old at the time of his death, having already passed through captivity, renunciation of a crown, entrance into the Franciscan Order and episcopal consecration. Reports of miracles at his tomb began to circulate soon afterward, including healings and other signs that were collected in a book of miracles associated with his cult. His body initially rested in Provence, and his relics later became the object of contention and translation, at one point being transferred from Marseille to Valencia by Aragonese forces, consolidating his status as a patron in both southern France and the Crown of Aragon.

    The process leading to Louis's canonization unfolded rapidly by medieval standards. Pope John XXII, himself a former teacher of Louis and a pope with strong ties to the Franciscan movement, canonized him in 1317, making him the third member of the Order of Friars Minor to be formally declared a saint after Francis of Assisi and Anthony of Padua. This canonization responded to both genuine popular veneration and the active promotion of his cause by his family, notably his brother King Robert of Naples, who had inherited the throne renounced by Louis and had an interest in enhancing the prestige of the Angevin dynasty.

    Liturgically his feast was fixed on 19 August, the anniversary of his death, and he was honored especially in Franciscan circles, in the Angevin domains and in regions connected with his life, such as Toulouse, Provence and Hungary. Over time he came to be invoked as a patron of youth, of those who renounce worldly status for religious life and of certain cities, including Valencia, where his relics were ultimately enshrined. His canonization also fed into broader debates within the Church about poverty and hierarchy, as his life seemed to show the compatibility-and tension-between Franciscan ideals and high ecclesiastical office.

    Louis of Toulouse quickly became a favored subject for artists, especially in regions under Angevin influence, and his image played a significant role in late medieval and early Trecento visual culture. He is typically depicted in episcopal vestments-a mitre, a richly decorated cope often patterned with fleur-de-lis referencing his Capetian lineage, and sometimes a crozier-combined with Franciscan elements such as the cord of the friars or the brown habit visible under the liturgical garments. This blending of symbols visually articulates his double identity as prince-bishop and Franciscan friar, and many images include a crown placed at his feet or being handed to another, signifying his renunciation of royal power.

    One of the most famous representations is the monumental altarpiece of Saint Louis of Toulouse painted by Simone Martini around 1317-1319 for the church of San Francesco in Naples, in which Louis is enthroned as a bishop while placing a crown on the head of his brother Robert, thereby legitimizing the latter's kingship through the saint's gesture. The saint also appears in Sienese painting, for instance in works associated with Pietro and Ambrogio Lorenzetti, and in later Renaissance panels such as a depiction by Giovanni Antonio Pordenone, where he stands holding a book and crozier, his cope adorned with fleur-de-lis. Manuscript illuminations, like the Getty Museum's "Initial T: Saint Louis of Toulouse," further disseminated his iconography in liturgical and devotional books, reinforcing his association with episcopal office, Franciscan humility and dynastic sanctity.

  6. Louis the Pious, Emperor of the Carolingians

    Louis the Pious (born 778 as Ludovicus Pius; d. 840) ruled the Carolingian Empire from 814 to 840, succeeding Charlemagne during the pivotal transition from military expansion to ecclesiastical consolidation and reform. His epithet derived from ostentatious acts of piety, most notably his public penance at Attigny in 822, where he atoned for blinding his nephew Bernard of Italy — a brutal enforcement of succession that haunted his reign. Crowned co-emperor by Charlemagne in 813 and sole ruler from 814, Louis immediately purged Aachen's court of "dissolute" figures and destroyed pagan artifacts to enforce moral rigor. The 817 Ordinatio Imperii divided the realm among his sons — Lothair (co-emperor, Francia Media), Pepin (Aquitaine), and Louis the German (Bavaria) — prioritizing imperial unity under clerical oversight while sowing the familial discord that would define his later years. He championed Benedict of Aniane's reforms, standardizing Benedictine observance via the Aachen councils of 816–819, which directly elevated Fulda's scriptorium: Rabanus Maurus became abbot in 822, fostering the opus geminata tradition in which Candidus composed his paired prose-verse hagiographies. Louis intervened decisively in Fulda's 816–822 turmoil by deposing Abbot Ratgar for tyrannical rule and installing the conciliatory Eigil, whose biography Candidus later penned as reformist propaganda. Sons rebelled in 830 and 833, deposing Louis at Colmar; restored by 834, he revised partition arrangements in 837 to favour the newborn Charles the Bald, fuelling further civil war until his death near Ingelheim in 840. The subsequent 843 Treaty of Verdun partitioned the empire into West Francia, East Francia, and the Middle Kingdom, fragmenting Charlemagne's vision into proto-national realms.

  7. Louis VII, King of France ("the Younger")

    Louis VII, known as the Younger, was King of France from 1137 until his death in 1180; he was the sixth ruler of the Capetian dynasty and the last to bear the title of "King of the Franks." His forty-year reign was dominated by three major themes: his failed marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine, his disastrous participation in the Second Crusade, and his long-standing rivalry with Henry II of England, who seized the Aquitaine domains through Eleanor's second marriage.

    Louis was born around 1120 in Paris, the second son of Louis VI the Fat and Adelaide of Savoy. He was not destined for the throne: the eldest son, Philip, was the designated heir, and Louis was sent to receive an ecclesiastical education, entrusted to the canons of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, which left an indelible religious mark on him. In 1131, however, Philip died in a trivial accident - he was thrown from his horse by a stray pig that crossed his path - and Louis suddenly became heir to the throne, torn from the devout and ceremonious environment of the cloister to be plunged into the brutal reality of feudal politics. This rift between his religious calling and the demands of royal power shaped his entire personality: he was an intelligent and deeply pious man, but often hesitant and lacking the pragmatic toughness that medieval governance required.

    In July 1137, a few days before becoming king upon his father's death, Louis married Eleanor of Aquitaine, the richest and most powerful woman in Western Europe, heiress to a duchy covering nearly a third of France. The marriage had been arranged by his father, Louis VI, as a strategic move to unite the French crown with Aquitaine, and it was a brilliant political move - so much so that Louis used the composite title of "King of the Franks and Duke of Aquitaine" for years. On a personal level, things were more complex: Eleanor was lively, cultured, independent, and a lover of troubadours; Louis was austere, devout, and tormented by religious scruples. One of the first serious incidents of his reign was the burning of the church at Vitry-en-Perthois in 1143, during a military campaign in Champagne: the flames killed over a thousand civilians who had taken refuge there, and remorse for that massacre haunted Louis for years, driving him to seek redemption through the crusade.

    The Second Crusade (1147-1149)

    In 1147, heeding the call of Pope Eugene III and the fiery preaching of Bernard of Clairvaux, Louis set out for the Second Crusade alongside Eleanor, who brought with her a retinue of ladies and an Aquitanian military contingent. The expedition was accompanied by marital tensions that escalated into an open crisis in Antioch, where Eleanor spent long days in private with her uncle Raymond of Poitiers, prince of the city: chroniclers of the time insinuated an adulterous affair, and Louis, wounded and furious, literally dragged his wife away from the city at night. Pope Eugene III, meeting them upon their return to Tusculum in 1149, attempted to reconcile the couple as we have already seen, insisting that they sleep in the same bed, but the damage was irreparable. The crusade ended with the shameful abandonment of the siege of Damascus after only five days in July 1148, a military defeat for which contemporaries sought a scapegoat and found one, in part, in Eleanor.

    In 1152, the marriage of Louis and Eleanor was annulled on the pretext of consanguinity - both were descended from King Robert II of France - with the consent of a synod at Beaugency. Louis had fathered two daughters with his wife, Mary and Alice, but no male heir, and this was an urgent dynastic problem.

    The divorce was the most politically disastrous decision of his life: Eleanor was free, and just eight weeks after the annulment she married Henry Plantagenet, Count of Anjou and Duke of Normandy, who in 1154 became King of England under the name Henry II. With this marriage, Louis's French rival acquired not only Aquitaine but also the Angevin domains: the Kingdom of France suddenly found itself surrounded to the west, north, and south by a vast "Angevin Empire," ruled by a lord richer and more powerful than the king himself. Louis remarried twice - in 1154 to Constance of Castile, who bore him two daughters, and in 1160 to Adele of Champagne, who finally gave him the long-awaited male heir, the future Philip II Augustus.

    For the remainder of his reign, Louis never ceased to fight Henry II by every means at his disposal: open warfare, diplomacy, strategic marriages, and support for rebels within the Angevin kingdom. He supported the revolts of Henry's sons - Henry the Younger, Richard, and Geoffrey - during the great conflict of 1173-1174, seeking to dismantle the Angevin Empire from within. Domestically, Louis was a king who was relatively respectful of the autonomy of emerging cities: he encouraged the development of Capetian urban communes, granted charters of franchise to numerous cities, and maintained collaborative relations with the merchant bourgeoisie of Ile-de-France more systematically than his predecessors.

    He was also a supporter of the University of Paris in its embryonic form, protecting the right of students and professors to operate in the capital.

    Louis VII suffered a stroke in 1179, which partially paralyzed him and forced him to bring forward the coronation of his son Philip in Reims, a ceremony he was unable to attend. He died in Paris on September 18, 1180, at nearly sixty years of age, and was buried in the Abbey of Barbeau, which he himself had founded; his remains were transferred to the Basilica of Saint-Denis in 1817. Historiographical judgment of him has long been overshadowed by comparisons with his son Philip II Augustus, who built modern France, and with his rival Henry II, whose stature is beyond question. Yet Louis VII held the Kingdom of France together for forty-four years under extremely difficult circumstances, defended the papacy of Alexander III against Frederick Barbarossa, and upheld the Capetian principle of dynastic succession at a time when a single long-awaited male heir was enough to throw the entire monarchy into crisis.

  8. Ludovico Ariosto

    Ludovico Ariosto (8 September 1474 – 6 July 1533) was an Italian Renaissance poet, dramatist, and courtier best known as the author of the chivalric romance epic Orlando furioso. Born in Reggio Emilia into a noble but not wealthy family, he spent most of his life in Ferrara, at the court of the Este dynasty, where he developed into one of the defining literary figures of sixteenth‑century Italy.

    Ariosto was the eldest of ten children of Niccolò Ariosto, a minor noble and military governor, and Daria Malaguzzi. The family moved to Ferrara around 1483, when Niccolò entered the service of Duke Ercole I d'Este, exposing the young Ludovico to the vibrant cultural circle of the Ferrarese court. He studied law and humanities at the Studio of Ferrara, then the city's main university, and later attended private academies where he began writing poetry in both Latin and vernacular Italian, signalling his early commitment to literary life over a purely legal or administrative career.

    Because his father's death in 1500 left his large family in financial difficulty, Ariosto was forced to abandon a peaceful, scholarly life and instead seek positions at court. In 1503 he entered the service of Cardinal Ippolito d'Este, second son of Duke Ercole I, acting as a diplomat, secretary, and travelling companion on military and diplomatic missions, including the Ferrarese campaign against Venice and a tense journey to Rome during the papal–Ferrarese conflicts. After the cardinal's promotion to the bishopric of Buda in 1517, Ariosto passed into the service of Duke Alfonso I d'Este, who entrusted him with increasingly important administrative tasks, among them the governorship of the wild and turbulent Garfagnana region in northern Tuscany, where he managed to pacify local feuds and suppress banditry with relatively limited resources.

    While fulfilling his duties as a courtier and administrator, Ariosto wrote across several genres: lyric poetry, satires, comedies, and his monumental epic. His most famous work, Orlando furioso ("Orlando Enraged"), began to take shape around 1505 and was first published in 40 cantos in 1516, with expanded and revised editions issued in 1521 and 1532 (the latter containing 46 cantos and considered definitive). The poem continues the Carolingian–Breton cycle started by Matteo Maria Boiardo's Orlando innamorato, weaving together the wars of Charlemagne against the Saracens with multiple love stories, fantastical episodes, and a pervasive irony that both celebrates and subtly critiques the chivalric tradition.

    Ariosto's other significant works include five vernacular comedies — such as La Cassaria and I Suppositi — which helped shape the Italian Renaissance comedy that later influenced playwrights like Shakespeare, as well as a collection of Satires in terza rima that offer a personal and often bitter reflection on the burdens of court life, social injustice, and his own financial constraints. His use of the Italian vernacular for high literary forms, from the epic to drama, played a crucial role in consolidating Italian as a language of serious literary expression across Europe.

    Ariosto's personal life was marked by both affection and frustration. He fell in love with Alessandra Strozzi‑Benucci, a married woman, after meeting her in Florence around 1513; though free to marry after her husband's death in 1515, he never formalized the relationship, perhaps due to family and social pressures. He later married Alessandra Benucci, a widow of uncertain status, and lived with her in Ferrara, where he devoted his final years to tending a suburban garden and revising Orlando furioso into its definitive 1532 edition.

    In the same period he also became involved in the court's theatrical life, serving as director of the first organized repertory theatre in Europe, the Sala Grande di Corte, where he oversaw productions of his own comedies and helped standardize stage practice under Duke Alfonso's patronage. Ariosto died in Ferrara on 6 July 1533, a few months after the final edition of Orlando furioso appeared, having secured his reputation as one of the most influential poets of the Italian Renaissance.

    Orlando furioso quickly became a best‑seller and was widely read and imitated across Europe, inspiring later poets such as Torquato Tasso and Edmund Spenser, as well as painters and composers who took scenes from the poem as subjects for art and opera. Modern critics often regard the poem as the finest expression of Renaissance humanism fused with irony and psychological complexity, balancing heroic idealism with a clear awareness of human frailty. Ariosto's status as a central figure in the literary canon is reflected in the numerous statues, street names, and academic studies dedicated to him in Ferrara and Reggio Emilia, where he remains a focal point of local cultural memory.

M

  1. Manuel I Komnenos

    Manuel I Komnenos (28 November 1118 – 24 September 1180) was a Byzantine emperor of the twelfth century who reigned over a crucial turning point in the history of Byzantium and the Mediterranean. His reign saw the last flowering of the Komnenian restoration, during which the Byzantine Empire experienced a resurgence of military and economic power and enjoyed a cultural revival. He is the emperor in whose court John Kinnamos served as imperial secretary — the same family name as the Bishop of Paphos, Basil Kinnamos, who ordained Neophytos the Recluse and commissioned the Enkleistra frescoes — and his reign forms the indispensable imperial backdrop to the entire Komnenian artistic renaissance whose provincial expression the Enkleistra represents.

    Manuel was the fourth and youngest son of Emperor John II Komnenos and Irene of Hungary. He accompanied his father on military expeditions, and on one occasion led his personal attendants in a counterattack during the unsuccessful Siege of Neocaesarea (1140) against the Danishmendid Turks, which reversed the course of the engagement. John praised him as the "Saviour of the Romans," though also criticised his rashness. Manuel inherited the throne following his father's death in a freak hunting accident on 8 April 1143. John had passed over his elder son Isaac, deeming him too easily angered, and named Manuel his successor a few days before dying in Cilicia. Manuel raced back to Constantinople to secure the palace before his surviving brother could act, and was crowned emperor — the fourth ruler of the House of Komnenos.

    His first major test was the Second Crusade (1147–1149). Manuel was forced to accommodate the passage of two large armies, under Conrad III of Germany and Louis VII of France; despite tensions and outbreaks of violence, both left Byzantine territory with relatively little damage, and Manuel subsequently made favourable agreements with both rulers. He married strategically into western dynasties: his first wife was Bertha of Sulzbach (renamed Eirene, 1146), sister-in-law of Conrad III, who died in 1159; his second wife, married in 1161, was Maria of Antioch — a union that visibly embodied his sustained engagement with the Crusader world. He made alliances with Pope Adrian IV, invaded the Norman Kingdom of Sicily (unsuccessfully), and was the last Eastern Roman emperor to attempt reconquests in the western Mediterranean.

    Manuel's most spectacular eastern achievements came in the late 1150s. Following Reynald de Châtillon's attack on Byzantine Cyprus in 1156 — the very island where Neophytos had just established himself as a hermit the previous year — Manuel campaigned in Cilicia in 1158 and forced the submission of Antioch. He made a ceremonial entry into the city on horseback while the Prince of Antioch and King of Jerusalem walked behind him on foot, personally led his troops to defeat the Latin knights commanded by de Châtillon, and himself unhorsed two Italian knights. This triumph of 1159 represented the apex of Byzantine prestige in the Crusader world. Manuel established a Byzantine protectorate over the Crusader states of Outremer and participated in a combined invasion of Fatimid Egypt. In the Balkans, following his alliance with Béla III of Hungary, he became overlord of Serbia, Bosnia, and Croatia, and in 1167 Dalmatia, Croatia, and Bosnia were incorporated into the empire.

    The gravest miscalculation of his reign was his rupture with Venice. Resenting the exceptional commercial privileges Venice had held since the reign of his grandfather Alexios I, Manuel confiscated Venetian goods, property, and ships, and arrested some 10,000 traders throughout the empire in 1171. Alternative Italian states such as Genoa and Pisa were supported instead, but the effect on Venetian dominance was negligible. Venice sent a fleet to exact revenge; an immediate crisis was averted when the Venetian crews were struck down by plague during a diplomatic parley, but the long-term wound festered. Venice's desire for vengeance contributed materially to the catastrophe of the Fourth Crusade and the sack of Constantinople in 1204.

    Towards the end of his reign, Manuel's eastern achievements were compromised by a serious defeat at Myriokephalon on 17 September 1176. His army was trapped in a narrow pass in the Phrygian mountains; a massacre was only avoided through a peace settlement requiring the demolition of Byzantine fortresses at Dorylaeum and Sublaeum. Although he concluded a subsequent advantageous peace with Sultan Kilij Arslan II, Myriokephalon proved the final unsuccessful effort by the empire to recover the interior of Anatolia from the Turks, and created an enemy who would prove more than troublesome in the coming decades.

    Manuel was one of the most personally compelling of all Byzantine emperors, called ho Megas (ὁ Μέγας, "the Great") by the Greeks. He appears as the hero of a history written by his secretary John Kinnamos, in whom every virtue is attributed to him. His court was a place of unusual cultural openness, combining Byzantine learned tradition with western chivalric influences absorbed through decades of crusading contact. Manuel composed a defence of astrology to the Church Fathers, asserting its compatibility with Christian doctrine — a controversy in which the theologian Michael Glykas refuted his arguments, revealing an emperor willing to enter theological debate in his own name. Venetian and other Italian traders became resident in Constantinople in large numbers, and their presence, together with the numerous Latin mercenaries Manuel employed, helped to spread Byzantine technology, art, literature, and culture throughout the Roman Catholic West. The "rococo" court style of Constantinopolitan painting that flourished during his reign — the very manner that Theodoros Apseudis brought to the Enkleistra in Cyprus in 1183 — was the direct artistic product of this cosmopolitan court atmosphere.

    Manuel died on 24 September 1180, aged sixty-one, in Constantinople, succeeded by his eleven-year-old son Alexios II Komnenos with Maria of Antioch as regent. The succession crisis that followed was catastrophic: within three years Andronikos I Komnenos had seized power, had Maria of Antioch executed, strangled the young emperor, and assumed the throne himself — only to be overthrown and brutally killed in a popular uprising in 1185. The cultural flowering of Manuel's reign was nonetheless genuine and lasting. The Komnenian artistic style he patronised radiated from Constantinople to every corner of the Byzantine world and beyond — to Cyprus, to Sicily, to Venice, to the monasteries of Serbia and Russia — carrying the visual language of an empire that, even as it contracted militarily, continued to define the aesthetic horizon of the medieval Christian East.

  2. Martin IV, Pope

    Pope Martin IV was born Simon de Brion (also rendered Simon de Brie), most likely around 1210–1220, in the region of Brie or Touraine in northern France, though some sources point to Montpincon in Normandy as his birthplace. The precise date of his birth remains uncertain, as is common for ecclesiastical figures of his era. He came from a family of minor French nobility, a background that would prove decisive in shaping both his personality and his political allegiances throughout his life.

    He received an excellent education, studying theology and canon law in Paris, then the intellectual capital of Latin Christendom and home to the most celebrated cathedral school in Europe. His scholastic formation placed him squarely within the tradition of rigorous Parisian theology, contemporaneous with the great flowering of scholasticism that produced figures such as Bonaventure and Thomas Aquinas.

    Simon de Brion's early clerical career was marked by rapid advancement through the French royal administration. He became a canon at Rouen and subsequently at Paris, before entering the service of the French crown at the highest levels. He served as Keeper of the Royal Seal (Garde des Sceaux) and effectively as Chancellor of France under King Louis IX (Saint Louis) and subsequently under his son Philip III (Philip the Bold).

    His close relationship with the Capetian monarchy was formative. He witnessed at close range the saintly and crusading character of Louis IX, and he absorbed deeply the idea that the French crown and the papacy shared a providential mission in Christendom. This conviction would later translate, during his pontificate, into an almost unconditional alignment of papal policy with French Angevin interests.

    In 1261, Pope Urban IV — himself a Frenchman (Jacques Pantaleon of Troyes) — elevated Simon de Brion to the cardinalate, naming him Cardinal-Priest of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, one of the ancient titular churches of Rome. This appointment marked the definitive transition from royal administrator to prince of the Church.

    He served subsequently as papal legate in France on multiple occasions under Popes Urban IV and Clement IV, demonstrating considerable diplomatic skill in managing the complex relationship between the papacy and the French throne. One of his most consequential legations involved supporting the ambitions of Charles of Anjou, brother of Louis IX, in southern Italy — a political investment that would bear bitter fruit during his own pontificate.

    Pope Nicholas III (Giovanni Gaetano Orsini) died on August 22, 1280, at Soriano nel Cimino. The conclave that followed took place in Viterbo and was one of the most contentious of the thirteenth century. The College of Cardinals was deeply divided between a powerful Italian faction — determined to maintain Roman aristocratic control over the papacy — and the French cardinals, backed by the formidable influence of Charles of Anjou, the dominant political force in central and southern Italy.

    The deadlock lasted several months. It was eventually broken, at least in part, through pressure exerted by Charles of Anjou on the Italian cardinals. On February 22, 1281, Simon de Brion was elected pope and took the name Martin IV.

    The choice of name is noteworthy and involves a historical confusion that persisted through the Middle Ages: Popes Marinus I (882–884) and Marinus II (942–946) had been mistakenly identified in the official lists as Martinus II and Martinus III. As a result, Simon de Brion, adopting the name Martin, was actually only the second pope to bear that name since the genuine Martin I (649–655), though he styled himself Martin IV. This numbering anomaly was not corrected until modern times.

    At the time of his election, Simon de Brion was not yet in major holy orders — a not uncommon situation for high-ranking ecclesiastics of the era who had risen primarily through administrative rather than pastoral channels. He was accordingly ordained priest and then bishop in rapid succession, and consecrated as Supreme Pontiff on March 23, 1281, at Orvieto.

    Martin IV's pontificate lasted just over four years, from 1281 to 1285. It was dominated, almost from beginning to end, by the profound political crisis unleashed by the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 and by his close, often servile relationship with Charles I of Anjou, King of Sicily and Naples and Senator of Rome. Contemporaries and later historians alike recognized that Martin IV was, in many respects, less the autonomous leader of Christendom than an instrument of Angevin foreign policy dressed in papal vestments.

    From the very outset of his pontificate, Martin IV placed himself in the orbit of Charles of Anjou. He confirmed and extended Charles's position as Senator of Rome, a civic title that gave the Angevin king effective control of the city. This move alarmed many within the Italian ecclesiastical establishment, who had hoped for a more independent papacy after the death of the strongly pro-Roman Nicholas III.

    Martin IV never actually resided in Rome during his pontificate. His court was established variously at Orvieto, Montefiascone, and finally Perugia, where he would die. His inability or unwillingness to reside in Rome — largely due to the political turbulence of the city and the dominant Angevin influence — was itself a symptom of the weakened position of the Holy See as an autonomous political actor.

    One of Martin IV's most consequential early decisions was the repudiation of the ecclesiastical union achieved at the Second Council of Lyon (1274) under Pope Gregory X. That council had secured a formal, if largely nominal, reunion between the Roman Church and the Byzantine Church, engineered through the submission of Emperor Michael VIII Palaeologus (1259–1282), who had agreed to acknowledge papal primacy in exchange for political protection against Western aggression.

    The Lyonese union had been deeply unpopular in Constantinople, where the vast majority of clergy and laity regarded it as a betrayal of Orthodoxy. Michael VIII had been forced to impose it by authoritarian means, provoking fierce resistance from monks, bishops, and the general populace. Nevertheless, it had served its diplomatic purpose: it had stayed the hand of Charles of Anjou, who had been planning a massive military expedition to overthrow the Byzantine Empire and restore the Latin Empire of Constantinople, which had fallen to Michael in 1261.

    Martin IV, aligned with Charles's ambitions and uninterested in the theological niceties of Eastern Christianity, formally excommunicated Michael VIII Palaeologus in 1281, effectively nullifying the union of Lyon. This act removed the last diplomatic barrier to Charles of Anjou's projected crusade against Byzantium, a massive naval and military operation that was being assembled through the late months of 1281 and early 1282.

    Michael VIII, isolated and facing existential threat, responded through one of the most dramatic episodes of medieval political espionage: he provided financial and diplomatic support to the Sicilian conspiracy that would detonate the Vespers.

    The evening of March 30, 1282 — the Monday of Easter Week — witnessed one of the most dramatic popular uprisings of the Middle Ages. At the Church of the Holy Spirit (Santo Spirito) outside Palermo, a dispute between French soldiers and Sicilian townspeople erupted into a massacre. Within hours, the revolt had spread across the entire island. By dawn, thousands of French men, women, and children had been killed throughout Sicily, and the Angevin administration had been effectively annihilated.

    The Sicilian Vespers was not purely spontaneous. It was the product of years of resentment against the harsh and exploitative rule of Charles of Anjou, combined with secret encouragement from Michael VIII Palaeologus and the disaffected Sicilian nobleman John of Procida, who served as a covert agent weaving together a conspiracy involving Aragonese, Byzantine, and Sicilian interests.

    The political consequence was seismic. The Sicilians, unwilling to return to Angevin rule, offered the crown of Sicily to Peter III of Aragon, who was married to Constance, daughter of King Manfred of Sicily and granddaughter of Emperor Frederick II — and thus a legitimate claimant through the Hohenstaufen line. Peter landed in Sicily in August 1282 and was acclaimed king.

    Martin IV's response was unequivocal and catastrophic in its long-term consequences. He excommunicated Peter III of Aragon (November 1282), declared Peter deposed from all his kingdoms and dignities, called for a Crusade against Aragon offering the kingdom of Aragon to Charles of Valois, and placed Sicily under interdict.

    These measures were constitutionally audacious — the papacy claiming the power to depose a sovereign king and assign his kingdom to another — but politically hollow. The Crusade against Aragon was launched in 1284–1285 under Philip III of France, but proved a military disaster, ending in the retreat and death of Philip III at Perpignan in October 1285. Peter III of Aragon was not dislodged, and the War of the Sicilian Vespers would drag on for twenty years after Martin's death, finally settled by the Peace of Caltabellotta (1302).

    For the papacy, the Vespers crisis represented a catastrophic failure: the loss of Sicily to Angevin control, the collapse of the anti-Byzantine crusade project, and the exposure of the fatal weakness of a papacy too closely bound to a single secular power.

    Beyond the consuming Sicilian crisis, Martin IV attended to several matters of internal Church governance. He was a consistent supporter of the Mendicant orders — the Franciscans and Dominicans — whose role in preaching, inquisition, and university theology was a central feature of thirteenth-century Catholic life. He issued several privileges confirming and extending their rights against the often fierce opposition of the secular clergy and diocesan bishops.

    He also engaged with the ongoing debates about Franciscan poverty, though the most acute phase of the controversy over the usus pauper and the question of whether Christ and the Apostles had owned property would only come to a head under his successors. His general sympathy lay with the Franciscan cause.

    His pontificate saw no major ecumenical council, no landmark theological definition, and no significant liturgical reform. The political emergencies of his reign consumed virtually all available energy.

    Martin IV's posthumous reputation received its most memorable (and devastating) literary treatment from Dante Alighieri in the Commedia. In Purgatorio, Canto XXIV, Dante encounters the penitent souls of the gluttons, and the poet Forese Donati identifies among them:

    Ebbe la Santa Chiesa in le sue braccia: / dal Torso fu, e purga per digiuno / le anguille di Bolsena e la vernaccia.

    Dante places Martin IV among the gluttons, purging his excessive love of food — specifically eels from Lake Bolsena prepared in Vernaccia wine, a Ligurian white wine. The image, combining irony with political commentary, encapsulates Dante's judgment on a pope who, in the poet's view, had gorged himself on temporal pleasures and Angevin patronage while neglecting his spiritual duties. Whether the detail about the eels was literally true or a satirical invention, it lodged itself permanently in the cultural memory of the medieval papacy.

    Martin IV died at Perugia on March 28, 1285, having never returned to Rome during his entire pontificate. He was buried in the Cathedral of San Lorenzo in Perugia, where his tomb, bearing a fine Gothic effigy, can still be visited. The tomb is attributed to the workshop active in Perugia in the late thirteenth century, though precise attribution remains debated among art historians.

    He was succeeded by Honorius IV (Giacomo Savelli), elected May 2, 1285.

    Martin IV occupies a difficult place in the history of the medieval papacy. His pontificate coincided with a moment of maximum Angevin domination over the Holy See, a condition that seriously compromised the papacy's claim to stand above political factions as the universal arbiter of Christendom. His excommunication of Michael VIII — effectively burying the Union of Lyon — set back any prospect of genuine reconciliation between Rome and Constantinople for centuries. His crusade against Aragon, theologically and juridically dubious, ended in failure and embarrassment.

    Yet it would be unfair to dismiss him entirely. He was a man of genuine learning, long experience, and sincere personal piety. His tragedy was structural as much as personal: elected through Angevin influence, dependent on Angevin power for the security of the Papal States, he lacked the independence — or perhaps the will — to chart a course of his own.

    He reigned at the precise moment when the great edifice of thirteenth-century papal supremacy, built by Innocent III and Innocent IV, was beginning to show its deepest cracks. The Sicilian Vespers, which shattered the Angevin project of Mediterranean domination, also exposed the limits of a papacy that had subordinated itself to that project. In a sense, the catastrophe that overwhelmed Martin IV was the catastrophe of an entire era of papal history — the end of the confident, universalist papacy of the high Middle Ages, and the prelude to the Avignon captivity that would follow a generation later.

  3. Matilda of England, Duchess of Saxony and Bavaria (1156–1189)

    Matilda of England (June 1156 – June/July 1189) was an English princess of the House of Plantagenet and by marriage Duchess consort of Saxony and Bavaria from 1168 until her husband's deposition in 1180. Born as third child and eldest daughter of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, she was named after her paternal grandmother, Empress Matilda, and baptized shortly after birth in Holy Trinity Priory, Aldgate, by Theobald of Bec, Archbishop of Canterbury. Her siblings included Henry the Young King, Richard I (who became Richard Lionheart), Geoffrey II of Brittany, Eleanor of England (Queen of Castile), Joan (Queen of Sicily), and the future King John. Her mother Eleanor was the most culturally formidable woman in Europe; her father Henry II was the architect of the Angevin Empire. Into this family, defined by its ambitions, its quarrels, and its relentless political energy, Matilda was born as the eldest daughter — the first of the family's daughters to be deployed as a diplomatic instrument on the continental stage.

    The political logic of her marriage was worked out in the mid-1160s at the intersection of two converging crises. Upon the disputed Papal election of 1159 and the ensuing schism, Henry II established closer ties to the Holy Roman Empire, particularly when he came into conflict with Thomas Becket. Emperor Frederick Barbarossa sent the Cologne Archbishop Rainald of Dassel to negotiate an English–German matrimonial alliance, and Henry the Lion was chosen as a match for Matilda. Matilda was just nine years old when negotiations began in 1165. She left England in September 1167, and the wedding finally took place in Minden Cathedral on 1 February 1168. Her husband was 27 years older than her, the lord of a territory stretching from the Harz Mountains to the Baltic Sea; their official residence was Dankwarderode Castle at Brunswick, where the newlyweds had their wedding feast.

    In the early years of marriage, despite her youth, Matilda ruled the vast ducal estates in her husband's absence — a formulation that places a girl who arrived in Germany at eleven or twelve in charge of the administration of two major duchies while Henry pursued his campaigns in the east and his pilgrimage to Jerusalem. A bracteate coin issued around 1172 documents her formal status: it portrays Matilda alongside Henry the Lion enthroned, with her holding a lily-crowned sceptre denoting consors regni — co-ruling authority atypical for a foreign consort. To show the duchess enthroned and sceptred alongside her husband was a public, circulating statement of political legitimacy that her Plantagenet lineage, as daughter of a king and granddaughter of an empress, made entirely credible.

    Her children included Henry V (Count Palatine of the Rhine), Lothar of Bavaria, Otto IV, Holy Roman Emperor, and William of Winchester. Through her youngest son William she is an ancestress of the House of Hanover, which ascended the British throne in 1714 and continues as the British royal family to this day. In Germany, Henry and Matilda held a magnificent court at Dankwarderode Castle and had Brunswick Cathedral erected from 1173 onwards, dedicated to St Blaise and St John the Baptist and later also to St Thomas Becket — the cathedral consecrated by their eldest son on 29 December, the feast day of St Thomas, in an act of liturgical piety that simultaneously honoured the Plantagenet martyr and rehabilitated the reputation of the family whose member had caused his death. Matilda played an instrumental role in establishing the Becket cult in Saxony through her patronage, demonstrating to the world that her father had received the martyr's forgiveness.

    The crisis of 1180 — when Frederick Barbarossa stripped Henry of his duchies and invaded Saxony — placed Matilda in circumstances that tested both her courage and her political intelligence. She appealed to the Emperor's chivalry to end the siege of Brunswick; her success saved the city from destruction. In November 1181 Henry submitted to the forfeiture. Matilda declined the Emperor's offer to retain her dower lands in Lüneburg, opting instead to join her husband in exile with their children. The family arrived at the court of her father Henry II of England in autumn 1181. By the summer of 1182 they reached Argentan in Normandy, where Matilda became acquainted with the troubadour Bertran de Born, who, calling her "Elena" or "Lana," made her the object of his desire in two poems of courtly love, comparing her beauty to that of Helen of Troy. In 1185, when Henry's three-year banishment ended, Henry II achieved the restitution of the allodial lands of Brunswick, and Matilda returned there with her husband and children.

    Matilda's role in the commissioning of the Gospels of Henry the Lion was more than ceremonial. It is almost certain that, together with her husband, she was a patron and co-donor of the famous manuscript, created between 1175 and 1188 at Helmarshausen Abbey. The manuscript's iconographic programme makes this co-patronage visually explicit: the first miniature depicts the Duke and Duchess presenting the manuscript to the enthroned Virgin Mary, and the manuscript has been called the Gospels of Henry and Matilda. The Coronation miniature — the most genealogically ambitious image in the manuscript — shows the hands of God descending to crown both Henry and Matilda simultaneously, Matilda's Plantagenet ancestry displayed alongside Henry's Welf and imperial lineage, a statement of equivalence that places her as a full participant in the dynastic self-representation the manuscript embodies. Her son Henry of Brunswick's charter of 1223 describes "his dearest mother of most happy memory" as the sole donor of the altar dedicated to the Virgin in the church of St Blaise at Brunswick — suggesting that her contemporaries understood her role in the cathedral's patronage as having a distinct identity from that of her husband.

    In the spring of 1189, facing the emperor's renewed ultimatum — crusade or exile — Henry chose exile and returned to England, while Matilda and her children remained in Brunswick to defend his interests. She died there, aged thirty-three, in June or July 1189, and was buried in Brunswick Cathedral. Her father, King Henry II of England, died approximately eight days after her — almost certainly before the news of her death reached him in Normandy. Henry the Lion returned to Brunswick after Frederick Barbarossa's death in 1191 and died in 1195, wishing to rest on the right hand of his wife "both in life and in death." Their sarcophagi lie side by side in the crypt of Brunswick Cathedral, beneath the church they built together, beside the altar she donated, in the city she had governed in his absence since she was twelve years old.

  4. Michael Doukas Glabas Tarchaneiotes

    Michael Doukas Glabas Tarchaneiotes — also known as Michael Tarchaneiotes Glabas — was born around 1235 and died after 1304. His full name combined the surnames of several of Byzantium's most distinguished aristocratic lineages: the Doukai, whose imperial prestige dated to the eleventh century; the Glabas, a military clan of long standing; and the Tarchaneiotai, a family of probable Turkic origin that had been thoroughly hellenised and integrated into the Byzantine military aristocracy by the Komnenian period. The layering of these names was not merely ornamental — it mapped a man's position within the dense web of intermarriages, alliances, and social debts that constituted the ruling class of the restored Palaiologan empire.

    Michael Doukas Glabas Tarchaneiotes has often been confused, including in relatively modern studies, with the protovestiarios Michael Tarchaneiotes, a nephew of Michael VIII Palaiologos who was killed in 1283. The two men were contemporary, bore similar names, and served in overlapping theatres — a confusion that has affected the reliability of some older scholarship on both figures. The man known as Glabas was a different person entirely, of distinct though related aristocratic lineage.

    Glabas married Maria Doukaina Komnene Branaina Palaiologina. The genealogical wealth embedded in her name — Doukaína, Komnēnē, Branaína, Palaiológina — placed her among the interconnected dynasties of Byzantine high nobility, and the union substantially reinforced Glabas's position at the Palaiologan court. They had one daughter, who married into the extended Angelos-Komnenos-Branas clan, further weaving the family into the uppermost tier of the imperial aristocracy.

    Glabas is first mentioned around 1260, when he was assigned to capture the city of Mesembria on the Black Sea coast from the deposed Bulgarian tsar Mitso Asen. This initial assignment, at the very moment of the Palaiologan restoration following the recovery of Constantinople from the Latins in 1261, establishes the essential character of his career: a lifetime spent defending and extending the empire's northern and western frontiers.

    At the same time, he rose in the imperial hierarchy, occupying progressively higher titles: from primmikerios of the court (33rd in the hierarchy), he became megas papias (22nd), pinkernes (15th), megas konostaulos (12th), and finally, sometime between 1297 and 1304 — probably around 1302–1303 — protostrator (8th in the hierarchy), in essence the commander-in-chief of the army, as the nominally superior megas domestikos had by that time become an honorific post. This steady ascent through six distinct rungs of the imperial court hierarchy over more than four decades is a remarkable career trajectory that reflects both sustained military effectiveness and reliable political loyalty across two successive reigns.

    Glabas's military record opens with a sequence of striking successes against Bulgaria in the early years of the restored empire. Around 1263 he defeated a Bulgarian army at Bizye, fortified Brysis, and proceeded to capture the fortresses Skopos, Petra and Skopelos, and the cities of Agathopolis, Sozopolis, Debeltos and Anchialos. This string of Black Sea coastal operations consolidated Byzantine control over the strategically vital Thracian littoral and demonstrated a capacity for sustained offensive campaigning that would mark all his subsequent commands.

    He reappears in 1278–79, leading another campaign against Bulgaria, where a successful revolt against Tsar Constantine Tikh had placed Ivaylo on the throne. Emperor Michael VIII sent Glabas at the head of an army to put the exiled prince Ivan Asen III on the Bulgarian throne. Glabas managed to capture the Bulgarian capital Tarnovo, where he seized Ivaylo's Byzantine wife Maria and their son Michael. He then pursued Ivaylo to the fortress of Silistra, which he besieged but failed to take. The capture of Tarnovo — even if it could not be held — was a spectacular achievement that demonstrated an aggressive strategic vision.

    Glabas launched a raid against Serbia with some 4,000 Cumans in 1282, and fought against the Angevins in Albania around 1284. Sometime between 1284 and 1291, he was sent to Albania, where he fought against the Angevin kingdom of Naples and recovered Dyrrhachion, Kruja, and Kanina. The recovery of Dyrrhachion — modern Durrës — was a particularly significant strategic gain, as the city was the principal gateway between Constantinople and the Adriatic world.

    Later, possibly in 1292, he defeated the sebastokrator Theodore, younger brother of the ruler of Thessaly Constantine Doukas, and unsuccessfully besieged the Epirote capital, Ioannina. The failure at Ioannina was one of the rare setbacks in an otherwise successful record, and the Despotate of Epirus remained a persistent irritant on Byzantium's western flank.

    In 1297–1298, Glabas was named governor of the western part of the empire, with Thessaloniki as his seat, and sent to deal with the Serbs, who had been periodically attacking Byzantine holdings in Macedonia and Albania for over a decade. Despite his great military experience and a relatively strong army, Glabas was unable to make any headway as the Serbs relied on guerrilla tactics and refused a pitched battle. He accordingly advised Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos to conclude a peace agreement with Stephen Uroš II — counsel that was strategically prudent even if it could not be presented as a victory. The advice was accepted, and a dynastic settlement with Stefan Milutin followed.

    In 1304, Glabas was dispatched to counter a Bulgarian invasion under Tsar Theodore Svetoslav, which had taken several forts and cities along the Balkan Mountains and the Black Sea coast. According to a panegyric by the court poet Manuel Philes, he retook Roussokastron and Mesembria, rebuilt Anchialos, and forced the Bulgarians to withdraw behind the Balkan Mountains. The recapture of Mesembria — the very city that had been his first assignment some forty-four years earlier — gave his career a certain symmetrical completeness. He then fell ill and returned to Constantinople, while the co-emperor Michael IX Palaiologos assumed command. This campaign of 1304 was his last.

    The esteem in which his contemporaries held Glabas is unusually well documented. The historian Nikephoros Gregoras claims that his military experience made the other generals "look like children." Philes also records that he had written a now lost treatise on "various military topics," one of the last attested examples in the long tradition of Byzantine military manuals — confirming that Glabas was not merely a practitioner of war but a reflective student of it.

    The court poet Manuel Philes — the most prolific versifier of the early Palaiologan period — was intimately associated with Glabas and his wife throughout his career. His panegyrics on Glabas's military campaigns and his commemorative verses for the Pammakaristos chapel together constitute a sustained literary monument to the general and his family. Philes also composed works on works of art connected with their patronage, pieces of particular value for their bearing on Byzantine iconography, since the writer had before him the works he describes.

    It is not known precisely when Glabas died, but it was probably sometime between 1305 and 1308. Before his death, he became a monk — the adoption of monastic tonsure in anticipation of death being standard practice among Byzantine aristocrats of every generation, including emperors.

    It is above all as a patron of sacred architecture that Glabas has secured his permanent place in art history. He and his wife restored the Pammakaristos Church and handed it over to Patriarch John XII of Constantinople in 1293. The restoration of the main church was a substantial act of patronage in its own right — the Pammakaristos was one of the principal imperial monastery-churches of the capital.

    The parekklesion, dedicated to Christ the Word, was added to the south side of the Pammakaristos by Maria around 1310 to house the tomb of her husband. While attached to the main church, it was conceived as an independent church in miniature — a cross-in-square with an apse, a naos whose central bay was covered by a dome, and a narthex with a gallery topped by two domes. The tomb of Tarchaneiotes and his wife was under an arcosolium at the centre of the northern wall of the naos. Despite its small scale — the nave only twenty feet wide, the dome approximately six feet in diameter — the architecture is an extraordinary tower of elaborate arches and vaults, completely encrusted with marble and mosaic, achieving an intensely grand and mystical beauty in a very small space.

    A representation of the Pantocrator, surrounded by the prophets of the Old Testament — Moses, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, Micah, Joel, Zechariah, Obadiah, Habakkuk, Jonah, Malachi, Ezekiel, and Isaiah — fills the main dome. On the apse, Christ Hyperagathos is shown with the Virgin Mary and St. John the Baptist. The mosaics cannot be firmly dated through historical sources, but must date from around 1310, contemporary with those of the Chora Church. A twenty-three-line epitaph carved on the exterior string course, attributable to Manuel Philes, takes the form of a lament in which the bereaved widow addresses her late husband in her own voice. The integration of verse, architecture, mosaic, and funerary monument into a single coordinated programme of commemoration is one of the finest examples of Palaiologan aristocratic piety at its most sophisticated.

    The Pammakaristos was not the only monument of Glabas's generosity. In 1302–1303 he and his wife sponsored the restoration of a chapel to St. Euthymios in the Church of St. Demetrius in Thessaloniki, as well as the Prisklabetza Monastery at Prilep and the Atheniotissa Church in Constantinople, where he also funded the construction of a hospice. The chapel of St. Euthymios in Thessaloniki — a significant site in the context of the Macedonian School of painting — appears directly in recent art-historical scholarship: Vapheiades's 2019 reattribution of the Protaton frescoes proposes that one of the painters of the Pammakaristos was none other than the artist of that Thessalonian chapel, creating a direct artistic link between the two foundations of Glabas and his wife.

    Glabas's daughter, whose first name is not known, married Andronikos Asen, and became the great-great-grandmother of Byzantine emperors John VIII Palaiologos and Constantine XI Palaiologos — the last two reigning emperors of Byzantium before the Ottoman conquest of 1453. The family's bloodline thus ran directly to the final chapter of the empire's history.

    After Glabas's death, his widow Maria became the nun Martha. She devoted the remaining years of her life to completing the commemorative programme at the Pammakaristos, commissioning poets, supervising mosaicists, and shaping the monument that would keep her husband's memory alive. In this sense, the Pammakaristos parekklesion is as much her monument as his — the creation of a woman who transformed grief and piety into one of the masterworks of late Byzantine civilisation.

  5. Michael VIII Palaiologos

    Michael VIII Palaiologos was born in 1224 or 1225. A scion of several former imperial families — Doukas, Angelos, Komnenos — he spent much of his youth in the imperial palaces at Nicaea and Nicomedia. His full dynastic name — Michael Doukas Angelos Komnenos Palaiologos — mapped the genealogical prestige of Byzantium's greatest families onto a single individual, and that prestige would prove one of his most potent political instruments.

    His remarkable resourcefulness and talent for intrigue were revealed early. At the age of twenty-one he was charged by Emperor John III Vatatzes of Nicaea with treasonous conduct against the state, a charge from which he extricated himself by the force of his wit. During his years of service at the Nicaean court he rose through the military hierarchy, holding successively the titles of megas konostaulos, megas doux, and despotes. The Empire of Nicaea — the principal of the successor states that had emerged from the ruins of Byzantine power after the catastrophe of 1204, when the Fourth Crusade had sacked Constantinople and installed a Latin emperor — was the most powerful candidate to reconquer the imperial capital, and Michael aligned himself with that ambition from the first.

    On the death of Emperor Theodore II Laskaris in 1258, Michael was chosen regent for Theodore's six-year-old son John IV. Michael was, in fact, John's second cousin once removed, both descended from Empress Euphrosyne Doukaina Kamatera. He moved rapidly: on 1 January 1259, Palaiologos made himself co-emperor as Michael VIII. The usurpation required ideological justification, and Michael found it in the argument that the moment demanded a man, not a child. The legitimacy question would haunt him throughout his reign, and the reconquest of Constantinople from the Latins became not merely a military objective but a political necessity — the act that would transform a usurper into a restorer.

    The first great military test of his co-emperorship came quickly and was met brilliantly. After the Battle of Pelagonia in 1259 against an anti-Nicaean coalition — a victory achieved through military force and diplomatic manipulation that induced much of the enemy coalition to defect — Milutin was left free to pursue the reconquest. By 1259 the remnants of the Latin Empire were reduced to Constantinople and its immediate environs, isolated from both the remaining Latin states of Greece and from the Nicaeans' Greek rival, the Despotate of Epirus. The Genoese alliance, sealed by the Treaty of Nymphaeum in 1261, gave Byzantium the naval power to offset the Venetians, who had profited enormously from the Latin occupation and had every reason to resist its reversal.

    Whether as the result of Michael's carefully planned ruse or of accident or both, the great city fell to his general in July 1261. The agent of the reconquest was the general Alexios Strategopoulos, who discovered that the Latin garrison had largely departed on a naval expedition and seized the moment, entering through a little-known passage in the walls. The Latin emperor Baldwin II fled by sea, never to return. The Orthodox clergy staged a triumphant liturgy in Hagia Sophia on 15 August 1261. Restorers scraped away Latin plaster, revealing the Christ Pantocrator in the apex of the south-west vestibule and the Deesis above the Imperial Door. Michael VIII entered through the Golden Gate, walked preceded by the icon of the Hodegetria, and then proceeded on horseback to Hagia Sophia and the Great Palace — a ritual itinerary that reconsecrated the city through the emperor's procession as much as through military force.

    The reconquest secured the dynasty's future but did not resolve its original sin. John IV was left behind at Nicaea and was later blinded on Michael's orders on his eleventh birthday, 25 December 1261. The Patriarch Arsenios excommunicated Michael for the act, triggering the Arsenite Schism, an ecclesiastical crisis that divided the Orthodox clergy and plagued the empire for decades. A few Greeks, even at the moment of the reconquest, realised that the centre of gravity had shifted from Asia Minor to Europe — a concern that would prove fateful, leading to the neglect of the eastern frontiers and eventually to the conquest of all Asia Minor by the Turks.

    Michael spent vast amounts of money restoring Constantinople after half a century of neglect under the Latin emperors. He restored Hagia Sophia — entrusting the monk Rouchas with the task, involving the restoration of the ambo, the solea, and the bema, and the installation of a colossal mosaic of the Deesis in the south gallery — rebuilt the Blachernae Palace, strengthened the city walls, and founded new churches and monasteries. In 1265–1266, Patriarch Germanos III commissioned a precious silk textile representing the emperor as a "New Constantine," hung in the western area of Hagia Sophia. Near the Church of the Holy Apostles, Michael VIII erected a column topped with a sculpture as a symbolic foundation gesture recalling Late Antique emperors. His re-establishment of the University of Constantinople contributed to the Palaiologan Renaissance, the cultural flowering between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries.

    The reconquest that secured Michael's domestic position immediately created a new and potentially fatal external threat. A powerful Western coalition against Michael was organised in 1267 by the Treaty of Viterbo between the Pope, the former Latin emperor, the Latin prince of Achaea, and Charles of Anjou — King of Sicily and the most formidable military organiser in the western Mediterranean. Against this coalition, military means were insufficient. Michael's response was the most audacious diplomatic gamble of the century.

    The Union of Lyon between the Greek and Latin churches was largely the result of Michael's political aims. He initiated the negotiations and almost single-handedly attempted to force the union upon his empire, convinced it was the one effective means to avert the Angevin threat and induce the Holy See to restrain Charles. After long negotiations, Michael sent envoys to the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, where a union of the two Churches was declared. The Greeks looked upon this union — at which the Eastern patriarchs were not represented — as a fraud. His own sister was imprisoned for refusing to accept communion with the unionists. Monks, clergy, and laity alike regarded the subordination of the Orthodox Church to Rome as spiritual treason. The political calculation that had driven Michael to accept the union was invisible to those who experienced it only as a religious betrayal.

    The political logic of the union broke down when Charles secured the election of his own papal candidate, Martin IV, who excommunicated Michael and declared a crusade against the "schismatic" Greeks. By 1281, a coalition of Western powers, with Venetian naval support and papal blessing, seemed to be repeating the events leading to the Fourth Crusade. Michael's counter-diplomacy in this final crisis was his most spectacular achievement. What he had on his side — the result of his consummate diplomatic ability — was a secret agreement with the Hohenstaufen supporters in Sicily and, most importantly, a secret alliance with King Peter III of Aragon. Scholarship has shown that the revolt known as the Sicilian Vespers, which broke out in Palermo on 30–31 March 1282, was in part engineered by Michael, who supplied the rebels with money. The massacre of the French signalled the revolt against Charles, and Byzantium was saved from a second Latin occupation — Michael's final and greatest coup, achieved by engineering an uprising six hundred miles away.

    Michael VIII Palaiologos died on 11 December 1282, aged approximately fifty-eight, at Pachomion near Lysimachia, without receiving Orthodox burial rites, excommunicated by the Greek clergy for his imposition of the union. His son and successor Andronikos II repudiated the Union of Lyon at once. Michael VIII was the founder of the Palaiologan dynasty that would rule the Byzantine Empire until the Fall of Constantinople in 1453. He had transformed a rump state in western Anatolia into a restored empire centred on the greatest city in Christendom, and defended it against the most formidable military coalition the West had assembled since the Fourth Crusade. The historian Nikephoros Gregoras would call him the greatest emperor of the Palaiologans. Whether the trade of Constantinople for Anatolia was worth making is a question that Byzantine history continued to debate, in blood and territory, for the next two centuries.

  6. Misericordia Maggiore di Bergamo

    The Misericordia Maggiore di Bergamo, known by its centuries-old abbreviation as MIA, is the oldest institution in Bergamo, founded in 1265 as a spiritual and charitable association, and still operating today as a foundation. Its history, spanning nearly eight centuries of the city's past, intertwines Christian charity, artistic patronage, and the stewardship of Bergamo's greatest civic monument: the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore.

    The founding of MIA must be placed within the context of the great religious and associative ferment sweeping through 13th-century communal Italy in the aftermath of the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, when the urban laity sought organized forms to express their charitable vocation. In Bergamo, as in many other cities of the Po Valley, this impulse took shape in the birth of a lay confraternity. In 1265, the Dominican friar Pinamonte da Brembate—later venerated as Blessed—founded, together with a group of laypeople and with the support of the Dominican bishop Erbordo, the Consorzio della Misericordia Maggiore, dictating the ten chapters of its original rule.

    The explicit purpose of the foundation was twofold: the spiritual growth of the brothers and the systematic aid of the most vulnerable—the poor, destitute religious, hospitals, the sick, widows, and orphans. The initial income came from monetary and in-kind contributions from the brothers, to which a unique element was added: the collection of fines imposed on heretics, during a time of intense struggle against the Cathar and Waldensian movements present in the Lombardy region.

    The rule of 1265 reflects the Dominican spirituality of those years: the document stated that the confraternity was established "ad confirmationem et exaltationem sancte fidei catholicae et ad confusionem et depressionem hereticorum".

    As early as 1267, two years after its foundation, the MIA began to receive bequests of real estate. In 1272, a domus misericordiae is documented on the grounds of the church of Santa Maria Maggiore, the first physical link between the association and the basilica that would become its principal monument. From the end of the 13th century, the increase in donations—especially in the form of bequests of real estate—made it possible to establish a stable endowment capable of ensuring ongoing charitable work.

    In the 14th century, the MIA gradually expanded its scope of action. In 1337 and in 1361, it received the so-called legates de Apibus in favor of poor students, foreshadowing the commitment to education that would characterize the institution for centuries to come. The Misericordia became the main focal point of what historians call the 13th-century "charity revolution," providing comprehensive assistance throughout the city and the entire provincial territory, in collaboration with the municipal administration.

    The epochal turning point in the history of the MIA occurred on June 23, 1449, when the Senate and the Great Council of Bergamo, reserving the right of patronage, transferred the administration of the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore to the Consortium. The monument, built by a vow of the citizens in the 12th century and considered the "city's chapel", became from that moment on the "most noble and principal part" of the Consortium's activities. A few years later, on March 14, 1453, Pope Nicholas V confirmed the Consortium's autonomy with a papal bull, removing the basilica from episcopal jurisdiction and placing it directly under papal authority: a decision that would generate lasting tensions with the bishops of Bergamo.

    From that moment on, the Misericordia Maggiore and the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore effectively became one entity, so much so that the institution's official name became Consortium of the Misericordia and of the Church and Fabric of Santa Maria Maggiore. This arrangement spurred a surge in donations and bequests, often in exchange for the distribution of bread to the poor, grants to needy students, and memorial Masses celebrated by the numerous priests in the service of the Consortium.

    Bolstered by its substantial income from assets—estimated in 1626 at approximately 20,000 scudi annually, of which 15,000 were allocated to the poor—the MIA became one of the most important patrons of the arts in northern Lombardy. The flow of money from the Consortium's vast estates went in part toward the basilica's lavish decorations: the splendid tapestries, the late-Renaissance stuccoes, and, above all, the inlaid wooden choir screen—considered the most important work ever commissioned by the Congregation.

    This masterpiece, created between 1522 and 1555 by Giovan Francesco Capoferri based on cartoons by the Venetian painter Lorenzo Lotto, represents one of the absolute pinnacles of Italian 16th-century wood inlay art. The fact that the MIA archive preserves several autograph letters by Lorenzo Lotto—among the most valuable sources for reconstructing the relationship between the painter and his Bergamasque patrons—underscores the archival significance of the collection itself.

    It is interesting to note that the MIA archive also preserves 14 choir books and 5 manuscripts, of extraordinary value for the study of Bergamo's medieval written and musical culture.

    The growing need to ensure the liturgical services of the basilica led to the founding, in 1506, of a school for clerics. Over time, this evolved into a full-fledged Academy in 1556, and then again in 1770 into the Collegio Mariano, which foreshadowed the middle and high school in Piazza Rosate. For over two and a half centuries, therefore, the Misericordia Maggiore assumed the responsibility of managing the city's main public secondary school, at a time when education was largely entrusted to religious and charitable institutions rather than to the state. In this regard, the MIA enjoyed extensive privileges granted by the Venetian administration—which governed Bergamo from 1428 to 1797—and even by the papal curia.

    The end of the 18th century marked a profound turning point in the history of the MIA. With the French Revolution and the subsequent Napoleonic campaigns, the ancient Consortium lost much of its autonomy, merging in 1808 into the Congregation of Charity as part of the public administration.
