By the mid-eleventh century, however, the emirate had fragmented into warring factions — the Kalbid dynasty that had governed it had collapsed, and rival Arab emirs competed for power, some of them actively seeking Norman military assistance against their rivals. The papal schism of 1054, which hardened the boundary between Latin and Greek Christianity, gave the papacy an ideological incentive to support the recovery of the island for the Latin church.

    Roger crossed the Strait of Messina for the first time in 1061, capturing Messina within a year and establishing a bridgehead in the northeast of the island. The Battle of Cerami in 1063 was an early turning point — a significant Norman victory against a larger Muslim force that secured control of the region between Troina and Messina and demonstrated that the conquest was militarily feasible. It was celebrated in Norman chronicles with legendary embellishments, including the reported apparition of Saint George on the battlefield.

    Progress thereafter was measured and deliberate rather than swift. The terrain of Sicily, the distance from Norman supply bases in Calabria, and the persistent resistance of the Arab population meant that the conquest took thirty years to complete. The decisive moment came with the fall of Palermo on 10 January 1072, when Roger and Robert entered the city together after a combined land and sea blockade. At Palermo, Robert formally invested Roger as Count of Sicily under his authority as Duke of Apulia — an investiture that gave Roger an official title and the authority to govern the island in Robert's name, while Robert retained Messina and the Val Demone for himself. After Robert's departure for the Italian mainland, the remaining conquest fell entirely to Roger.

    Palermo fell in 1072, Trapani in 1077, Agrigento in 1087, and finally — after years of intermittent resistance — Enna and Noto in 1091, the last Arab stronghold. In the same year, Roger crossed to Malta, which capitulated with little resistance, completing the conquest of the central Mediterranean island group.

    Roger's administrative genius was, in the long run, as significant as his military achievements. He deliberately avoided the creation of numerous small feudal lordships, which had turned the Norman territories on the Italian mainland into a landscape of near-perpetual baronial rebellion. Large grants of land were made almost exclusively to the Catholic Church, whose institutional stability Roger correctly identified as the surest foundation for his own legitimacy. This policy of concentrating landed wealth in ecclesiastical hands while maintaining centralized comital authority over the nobility created the administrative conditions for the extraordinarily powerful royal government that his son Roger II would subsequently inherit and develop.

    His approach to the island's Muslim and Greek Christian populations was pragmatic and relatively tolerant. Rather than expelling or forcibly converting the Arab population — which constituted the overwhelming majority of the island's inhabitants — Roger permitted Muslims to continue practicing their faith, retain their property, and serve in his administration and army. Arabic remained a language of governance. Greek Orthodox monasteries continued to function alongside the new Latin bishoprics that Roger established at Syracuse, Agrigento, and elsewhere. This policy of multicultural coexistence was not idealism but state-craft: Roger needed the agricultural productivity and administrative expertise of his Arab subjects, and he needed the loyalty of the Greek Christian communities whose ecclesiastical traditions predated the Arab conquest.

    His relationship with the papacy was one of the most carefully managed dimensions of his reign. In 1098, Pope Urban II — whom Roger had sheltered and supported during the crisis of the anti-pope Clement III — granted Roger and his heirs the apostolic legateship of Sicily, a remarkable concession that gave the count virtually the powers of a papal legate over the Sicilian church, including the right to appoint bishops personally without reference to Rome. This privilege, known as the Monarchia Sicula, became one of the most jealously guarded prerogatives of the Sicilian crown and was still being disputed between the papacy and the kings of Sicily in the seventeenth century.

    Roger married three times. His first wife was Judith of Évreux (married c. 1062), who died in 1076. His second wife was Eremburga of Mortain (married 1077), who died in 1087. His third and most consequential marriage was to Adelaide del Vasto (married 1089), a noblewoman of Lombard Aleramici origin from Piedmont, who bore him three children who survived to adulthood: Simon, Constance, and — born on 22 December 1095 — the future Roger II. It was Adelaide who served as regent of Sicily after Roger's death and oversaw the education of the young Roger II in the cosmopolitan Palermo court.

    Roger died at Mileto in Calabria on 22 June 1101, at approximately seventy years of age — remarkable longevity for a man who had spent four decades in almost continuous military campaigning. He was buried at the abbey of Sant'Eufemia in Calabria, a Benedictine monastery he had himself founded. The state he left behind him was the County of Sicily and Calabria — not yet a kingdom, but already the wealthiest and most sophisticated polity in southern Italy, and the seedbed from which, under his son, the first genuinely multicultural medieval monarchy of Western Europe would grow.

  4. Roger II of Sicily (Roger the Great, Ruggero II)

    Roger II of Sicily, also known as Roger the Great (Ruggero II), was one of the most remarkable monarchs of the medieval world, ruling a multicultural kingdom that blended Norman, Byzantine, Arab, and Latin traditions into a singular and sophisticated civilization. Born on 22 December 1095, he died on 26 February 1154, leaving behind a state that shaped southern Italy for centuries.

    He was the son of Roger I of Sicily, the Norman conqueror who had wrested the island from Arab rule, and Adelaide del Vasto. Upon the death of his elder brother Simon in 1105, the nine-year-old Roger inherited the County of Sicily under the regency of his mother. Educated by Greek and Arab tutors at the cosmopolitan court of Palermo, he grew up in an environment where Italian, Arabic, Greek, and Norman French circulated together, an experience that deeply informed his later policies.

    Roger assumed personal control of the county around 1112 and quickly demonstrated the political and military skill that would define his reign. By 1122, he had absorbed all of Calabria on the mainland. When Duke William of Apulia died without an heir in 1127, Roger claimed the duchy, overcoming baronial resistance and papal reluctance to accept a powerful southern state.

    The decisive turn in Roger's career came during the papal schism of 1130, when Innocent II and Antipope Anacletus II contested the papal throne. Roger backed Anacletus and in return received a bull dated 27 September 1130 that elevated him to kingship. He was crowned King of Sicily on Christmas Day 1130 in Palermo Cathedral, becoming the first ruler of a kingdom that endured for centuries.

    After Anacletus's death in 1138, Roger's position became precarious, but in 1139 he defeated Innocent II's forces at Galluccio, captured the pope, and compelled recognition of his title as rex Siciliae ducatus Apuliae et principatus Capuae, King of Sicily, Duke of Apulia, and Prince of Capua, through the Treaty of Mignano. The framework established there defined the political geography of southern Italy into the modern era.

    Roger was not only a conqueror but also a major institutional builder. He promoted legal reforms that strengthened royal and bureaucratic authority while curbing recurrent feudal rebellion, and he advanced a standardized coinage, the ducat, associated with the Duchy of Apulia. His administration operated in Latin, Greek, and Arabic, with Greek and Arab officials serving alongside Norman elites, making his state one of the most sophisticated political systems in twelfth-century Europe.

    His ambitions extended across the Mediterranean. With a powerful fleet led by admirals styled emirs, most famously George of Antioch, Roger launched campaigns on the North African coast: Tripoli fell in 1146 and Cape Bona in 1148, earning him the additional title of King of Africa. These possessions were later lost under William I, but they reveal Roger's broader imperial vision centered on Sicily.

    Roger's artistic patronage is central to medieval art history. The Cappella Palatina in Palermo, begun around 1130, remains the most celebrated monument of his reign, combining Saracenic muqarnas, Byzantine gold mosaics, and Latin architectural structure into a coherent royal statement. The mosaic in Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio (La Martorana), showing Roger crowned directly by Christ in Byzantine imperial mode, articulated a potent theology of kingship. His royal mantle, now in the Imperial Treasury in Vienna, bears Arabic embroidery dated 528 AH (1133-34), a rare and material witness to the court's cultural synthesis.

    Roger II died in Palermo on 26 February 1154 at the age of fifty-eight and was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus in Palermo Cathedral. He was succeeded by his son William I. The kingdom he forged, where Muslim scholars, Greek monks, Norman knights, and Jewish merchants coexisted under one crown, remains one of the most distinctive political and cultural experiments of medieval Europe.

  5. Roman Linearism

    In Roman art history, the term "Roman linearism" is not a standard, widely recognized stylistic category like verism or classicizing style; instead, it usually refers informally to the way Roman painters handled contour lines and spatial construction in frescoes and panel paintings, particularly in domestic and architectural illusionism (e.g., Pompeian wall-painting). It is best understood as a descriptive shorthand for the linear logic they used to suggest depth, volume, and continuity rather than a single, codified "school" of style. In Roman interior painting, especially in the Second and Fourth Pompeian Styles, artists relied heavily on silhouettes and incised contours to define columns, cornices, balustrades, and architectural frames that recede into the "picture-space." These linear elements are not coherently bound to a single horizon line in the Renaissance sense of linear perspective; instead, they follow a kind of pragmatic, multiple-horizon optics, where each architectural zone has its own implied vanishing-point axis. This produces a layered, almost "stage-set" effect, in which lines cluster to suggest depth without enforcing a single, mathematically unified vanishing system.

    In the Middle Ages "Roman linearism" is best read as a shorthand for how Roman-derived linear and spatial habits survived, mutated, and were re-encoded in medieval art. In practice, this lineage appears in three main ways: the inheritance of Roman contour-driven modeling, the persistence of Roman architectural illusionism in early Christian and Romanesque spaces, and the transmission of Roman linearity into manuscript illumination and panel painting. In illuminated manuscripts from the ninth to the thirteenth century, "Roman linearism" manifests as a continuity of contour-based drawing and patterned space. Carolingian and Romanesque initials, narrative scenes, and marginal figures often rely on strong, rhythmic lines to define drapery, bodies, and architectural frames, rather than on a consistent, unified illusion of depth.

S

  1. Scrovegni, Enrico degli

    Enrico degli Scrovegni was a wealthy Paduan banker, moneylender, political actor, and art patron whose historical importance rests above all on the monument he commissioned: the Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel in Padua, decorated by Giotto and regarded as one of the foundational works of Western painting. Born in Padua, he was the son of Reginaldo (Rinaldo/Rainaldo) degli Scrovegni and Capellina Malacapelli, and inherited both extraordinary wealth and a deeply compromised family reputation tied to usury.

    Reginaldo's notoriety became literary memory when Dante placed him among the usurers in the seventh circle of Inferno. Enrico inherited the family business and expanded it within the financial and political structures of the Paduan commune, while also seeking social rehabilitation through strategic alliances and religious patronage. Sources connect him to major regional dynasties through marriage ties with the Carrara and Este families, and to the factional instability of early fourteenth-century Veneto politics.

    Around 1300, near the Roman arena in Padua, Enrico acquired land for a large family complex and built a private chapel dedicated to Santa Maria della Carita. He commissioned Giotto to decorate it, and the frescoes executed circa 1303-1305 present a unified cycle of the Life of the Virgin, the Life of Christ, and the Last Judgment. In the latter, Enrico is represented offering a model of the chapel to the Virgin, a highly charged image of patronage, devotion, and hoped-for salvation.

    Scholars have long debated whether the commission was principally penitential, intended to atone for personal and familial sin, or also an assertion of status and dynastic memory. The chronology shows that Giotto's cycle predates the composition of Dante's Inferno, so the chapel cannot be read as a direct reply to Dante's condemnation. At the same time, its scale, cost, and function as a family burial space indicate that expiation, commemoration, and public prestige all converged in the project.

    Enrico later became entangled in changing regional power struggles: he left Padua for Venice in 1320, was formally banished in 1328, and died in Venice in 1336 after establishing new financial operations there. Despite exile, he ordered that his body be returned to Padua and buried in his chapel. His tomb remains in the apse, and a notably lifelike sculpted portrait, attributed to the Master of the Scrovegni and Salomone Tombs, survives in the sacristy. Enrico is therefore remembered less as a financier than as the patron who made possible Giotto's decisive reconfiguration of pictorial language at the beginning of the Trecento.

  2. Simone della Tosa (c. 1300 - Florence, 24 October 1380)

    Florentine magnate, office-holder, and annalist

    The Della Tosa, or Tosinghi, held jointly and by hereditary right with the Visdomini and the Aliotti the dignity of visdomini of the Florentine bishopric: the administration of episcopal temporalities during a vacancy of the see, together with the ceremonial responsibilities attending a new bishop's entry into Florence and his installation. For Simone, the office was more than a source of income and forms the connective tissue between his public life and his writing.

    Simone is named among the protectors of the bishopric in the Bullettone, the consorteria's register of episcopal goods, rights, and precedents, under the date 14 May 1323, and again in 1325, when the reigning bishop confirmed to the three houses their traditional honours. Bonanno names the bishop of 1325 as Acciaiuoli; since Angelo Acciaiuoli held the see only from 1342, this is very likely a slip in the DBI text and the reference is instead to Francesco Silvestri. The point should be checked against the Bullettone itself.

    Simone's recorded service falls in the decades of Florence's costly and ultimately unsuccessful bid for Guelf hegemony in Tuscany. His offices were administrative, diplomatic, and military rather than deliberative, the range available to a magnate under the Ordinances of Justice.

    • May 1324 - guardiano of the fortress of San Miniato.
    • December 1328 - accompanies Pino della Tosa, his consorte, to Bologna on a communal embassy to Cardinal Bertrand du Poujet, papal legate in Lombardy, in connection with the mutiny of German knights against Louis the Bavarian.
    • May 1329 - accompanies messer Simone di Rosso della Tosa on an embassy to Volterra to negotiate peace with Pisa.
    • 7 September 1330 - posted, again with Simone di Rosso, to garrison Carmignano.
    • July 1331 - serves in the office of the Condotta.
    • February 1332 - sent to Serravalle.
    • 5 June 1335 - at Pisa with Lorenzo di Nello.
    • January 1336 - at Perugia with Pino della Tosa at the outbreak of the war with Mastino della Scala, lord of Verona.
    • May 1337 - captain of the pavesari grossi during the Florentine devastation of the Lucchese contado.
    • August 1337 - at the castle of Vernio with Iacopo Ciccioni.
    • 4 August 1342 - present in Florence, by the traditional prerogative of his consorteria, at the entry of the new bishop Angelo Acciaiuoli.
    • September 1343 - 11 June 1344 - podestà of Poggibonsi.
    • 1350 - ambassador to Modena, the one commission he does not record in his own Annali.

    Alongside these offices, the Annali register the management of his patrimony, enlarged by purchases of land at Travalle, at Sesto, and in the pieve of San Niccolò a Calenzano. In 1336 he paid 300 gold florins to discharge a fine imposed on his brother Francesco under anti-magnate legislation.

    On 25 October 1370, as an old man, Simone petitioned the Signoria for the status of popolano. Bonanno shows that this was not a break with his consorts: his kinsmen had already crossed from magnate to popular status, taking the new surname Biligiardi, and the petition itself states that only Simone and two nephews - Niccolò di Giovanni and Lodovico di messer Bindo - remained inscribed among the magnates. He was admitted by a narrow margin, with access to all offices of the Republic except the Signoria and the Collegi, a restriction standard in such petitions from 1361.

    Manni reports that on this occasion he assumed a new coat of arms, which he later directed by will to be carved on his tomb in Santa Maria Novella and painted on three priestly chasubles for Santa Maria Novella, Santa Reparata, and a third church to be chosen by his son Baldo, who would become a knight and rise to the priorate. That he was the last of his house to relinquish magnate status, and that he composed a memorandum for the perpetuation of his consorteria's episcopal privileges, together mark an unusually tenacious attachment to the traditions of an old lineage.

    On 17 October 1377, taking advantage of confiscations during the War of the Eight Saints, Simone bought from the Commune, for 170 gold florins, a house and farmland belonging to the pieve of San Martino a Sesto. On 20 July 1378 his name appears in the chronicles among the citizens knighted by the insurgent Ciompi, but he was not among those who later accepted the Signoria's confirmation of the new dignity. On 21 October 1380 he made his will, restored the ecclesiastical goods acquired three years earlier, and posted a usury bond acknowledging that he had been a public usurer and promising restitution of his gains from lending at interest. He made his son Baldo universal heir, with a third of the estate to go to his sister Margherita should Baldo die without male issue, and a codicil assigned his share of the houses and shops held with the consorts to his nephew Niccolò di Giovanni di Baldo, keeping consortial property in the male line. He died at Florence on 24 October 1380, three days after making his will.

    A caution for prosopographers: Gaetano Salvemini, in La dignità cavalleresca nel Comune di Firenze (1896), lists Simone among knights created on 20 January 1382. Bonanno notes that he had then been dead for two years; the knight is his son Baldo, on the testimony of Marchionne di Coppo Stefani. Simone's memory rests chiefly on the Annali fiorentini, a list of consuls and podestà from 1196 to 1278 followed by annalistic notices and private ricordi from 1115 to 1346, with a lacuna between 1310 and 1323. The period of composition is unknown. The work belongs to the dense, mutually contaminated corpus of Florentine cronichette, is reliable in its factual indications, and was described by Natalino Sapegno as rigid in style and dry in content. For the historian of art and architecture, it is especially valuable for the dating of the first loggia of Or San Michele to 1284 and for its notices of Arno floods.

    The Annali were printed by Domenico Maria Manni in Cronichette antiche di varj scrittori del buon secolo della lingua toscana (Florence, 1733), and a further edition appeared in Milan in 1844. In the same volume Manni assembled biographical notices on the author from archival documents. His remains the edition in general scholarly use, though it is not critical: modernizing orthography has been shown to account for many divergences between print and manuscript. A critical edition by Silvia Cagnizi, Simone della Tosa, Annali fiorentini. Edizione critica (University of Padua, 2017), should be verified before citation.

    A second work survives in an eighteenth-century copy: the Memoriale del vescovado di Firenze in sede vacante scritto da Simone della Tosa l'anno MCCCLXX (Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Manoscritti, 167, cc. 39r-55v). It sets out the office of the visdomini - custody of episcopal temporalities during a vacancy, ceremonial functions at the entry of a bishop-elect, and the privileges of the visdominato - and closes with an enumeration of episcopal notaries. Simone says plainly that it should serve as instruction and record for the houses of the Visdomini, Tosinghi, and Aliotti whenever the see falls vacant.

  3. Simone Saltarelli, Archbishop of Pisa (c. 1262–1342)

    Simone Saltarelli was a Florentine Dominican friar who rose through the ranks of his order to become bishop of Parma and then archbishop of Pisa, a see he held for nearly twenty turbulent years. He is remembered both as a churchman who steered Pisa through occupation and exile, and as a patron whose commissions - above all the frescoes of the Camposanto and his own tomb in the church of Santa Caterina - remain landmarks of Trecento art.

    Florentine origins and Dominican formation

    Saltarelli was born in Florence around 1262, the son of Guido Saltarelli, whose family originated from Monte di Croce in the lower Val di Sieve. His brother Lapo Saltarelli was a White Guelf jurist and politician whom Dante, no admirer, named among the corrupt in the Paradiso (canto XV, line 128).

    In 1281 Simone entered the Dominican convent of Santa Maria Novella in Florence, the house with which he would keep close ties for the rest of his life. After his formation he taught as lector in the order's schools, at Lucca in 1288 and at Arezzo in 1292. Between 1298 and 1316 his career within the Order of Preachers accelerated: he served as prior of Santa Maria Novella from 1300, represented his province at general chapters in Marseille, Genoa, and Bologna, and from around 1307 acted as chaplain and household cleric to Cardinal Napoleone Orsini, whom he assisted as a papal legate in Tuscany, Romagna, and the Trevigiano. By 1314 he was procurator general of the Dominican Order, its chief representative at the papal curia.

    On 7 September 1316, shortly after his election, Pope John XXII named Saltarelli bishop of Parma. He arrived in the city in February 1317 and devoted his episcopate largely to civic pacification - a local chronicle records that he had the cathedral bell rung each morning to call the faithful to pray for Parma's peace, so that it became known as the "bell of peace." After 1320 he supported the papal legate Bertrando del Poggetto in his campaign against the Visconti in Emilia.

    In 1323 Saltarelli was transferred to the archdiocese of Pisa, succeeding Oddone della Sala, whose long conflict with the commune had made his position untenable. He received the pallium from three cardinal-deacons - Napoleone Orsini, Giacomo Stefaneschi, and Luca Fieschi - on 6 July 1323, but remained at Avignon for another year, sending his vicar and his nephew Tommaso di Bino ahead to take possession of the archiepiscopal palace on 26 October 1323. He himself reached Pisa only in October 1324, once a war between Pisa and Aragon over Sardinia had been settled.

    As archbishop, Saltarelli pursued a conciliatory course, confirming the synodal constitutions of his predecessor and working to align Pisan policy with Florence, a shift that also benefited his own family: in 1326 the confiscated property of his brother Lapo was restored.

    Saltarelli's governance was interrupted by the invasion of Emperor Louis of Bavaria, who entered Tuscany with Castruccio Castracani's support and besieged Pisa. The archbishop urged resistance, but Louis entered the city on 11 October 1327 and Saltarelli fled - first to Siena, then to Massa Marittima, where in January 1328 he drafted a detailed memorandum in his own defense, and eventually to Avignon. There he is documented from January 1329, surviving on the administration of the abbey of Pomposa and a benefice near Fiesole granted by the pope.

    Pisa expelled the imperial vicar on 17 June 1329 and returned to papal obedience; Saltarelli, together with the bishop of Lucca, later helped hand the antipope Nicholas V over to John XXII in July 1330. His nephew returned to Pisa in August 1329, and Saltarelli himself followed in January 1330. He spent his remaining years managing the delicate politics of the city's new rulers, the Della Gherardesca and Gualandi Maccaione factions, and in November 1339 personally visited the suffragan diocese of Massa Marittima - the first archbishop, a contemporary chronicler noted, ever to have done so.

    Saltarelli's name is inseparable from the Camposanto monumentale of Pisa, whose fresco cycle - including the celebrated Triumph of Death - was long attributed to Buonamico Buffalmacco and is now more cautiously assigned by scholars to an anonymous "Master of the Triumph of Death" (a name proposed after the historian Michele Luzzati's 1988 study linking the cycle's Dominican iconographic program to Saltarelli's patronage). Modern art historians remain divided over the attribution, with Francesco Traini also proposed as a candidate, but the consensus that Saltarelli shaped the theological program of the frescoes, painted around 1336, has held. He also maintained close ties to Santa Maria Novella in Florence, fitting out rooms there for his own use in 1337 and, around 1340, donating liturgical furnishings and study books to several convents of the Roman Dominican province. In 1342 he had the church and convent of Santa Marta built in Pisa for Dominican nuns.

    Simone Saltarelli died on 24 September 1342. He chose burial in the Dominican church of Santa Caterina in Pisa, where his nephew Michele di Bino commissioned the workshop of Andrea, Nino, and Tommaso Pisano to carve his funerary monument - today considered one of the masterpieces of Trecento Pisan sculpture, though it now stands in a different position from its original placement. The reliefs beneath the recumbent effigy are thought to illustrate the virtuous deeds attributed to Saltarelli in the necrology of Santa Maria Novella. So well regarded was he in Pisa that, on his death, both the cathedral chapter and the commune asked the pope to appoint another Dominican, Marco Roncioni, as his successor; Clement VI instead transferred Dino da Radicofani, archbishop of Genoa, to the see.

  4. Societa dei Toschi (Societa de' Toschi)

    The Societa dei Toschi (also written Societa de' Toschi) refers to a specific military and foreigners' guild in Bologna, active primarily between the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and not simply to a general association of people surnamed Toschi.

    In medieval Bologna, the Societa de' Toschi functioned as a military company and guild of Tuscan citizens residing in the city, identified precisely as toschi, that is, foreigners of Tuscan origin. These societies possessed statutes, internal magistracies, and their own armament, operating in part as military groups and in part as social and political associations.

    The Toschi represented one of the largest foreign communities in Bologna, due both to geographical proximity to Tuscany and to migratory inflows linked to Guelf-Ghibelline conflicts. The Societa de' Toschi became involved in urban political dynamics, acting as a significant lobbying group and armed force, with connected families assuming prominent roles within the republican institutions of the Bolognese commune during the early thirteenth century.

    The Torre Toschi, now in Piazza Minghetti, is traditionally associated with this community: it was most likely built by a Guelf branch of the Toschi family that emerged within the context of that military society. Although the tower later passed to the Passipoveri, then the Cazzanemici, and later the Locatelli, it remains the most visible architectural symbol of the political and social influence of the Societa dei Toschi in medieval Bologna.

  5. Stefan Uroš II Milutin Nemanjić

    King Stefan Uroš II Milutin Nemanjić was born around 1254–1255 as the second son of King Uroš I Nemanjić and Queen Helen. He was the seventh ruler of the Nemanjić dynasty — the ruling house that had governed Serbia since the late twelfth century, when Stefan Nemanja had forged a unified Serbian state and his son St. Sava had given it an autocephalous Orthodox Church. The dynasty's identity was inseparable from its religious mission: each Nemanjić king was simultaneously a political sovereign and a protector of Orthodoxy, a role that the Church reinforced through hagiography, liturgy, and the monumental art of the endowment churches.

    According to the Lives of Serbian Kings and Archbishops by his contemporary Archbishop Danilo II, a conflict broke out between his father King Uroš I and his brother King Stefan Uroš Dragutin in 1276. King Uroš I abdicated and died less than two years later. Six years later, following a riding accident, King Dragutin abdicated in favour of his younger brother during the council of Deževo in 1282. The circumstances of Milutin's accession were thus already entangled in the dynastic tensions that would shadow his entire reign: he came to power not by primogeniture but through the incapacity of a brother who retained substantial northern territories and a claim that his own heirs could one day press.

    Together with his great-grandfather Stefan Nemanja, the founder of the Nemanjić dynasty, and his grandson Emperor Stefan Uroš IV Dušan, King Milutin is considered the most powerful ruler of the Nemanjić dynasty. This assessment reflects a reign of thirty-nine years that transformed Serbia from a regional power into the dominant force in the Balkans — doubling the kingdom's territory, reorienting its cultural identity towards Byzantium, and laying the foundations of economic prosperity that would make the Serbia of Dušan the wealthiest state in the region.

    The first seventeen years of Milutin's reign were defined above all by sustained military pressure on Byzantine Macedonia. The ailing empire of Andronikos II, stripped of its army and its navy, could offer only sporadic resistance. Milutin advanced systematically down the Vardar valley, seizing towns, fortresses, and entire regions that had been Byzantine for centuries. In 1284, Milutin also gained control of northern Albania and the city of Dyrrachion — the same port that his contemporary Michael Glabas Tarchaneiotes had also contested — demonstrating the breadth of his strategic ambition across both the Aegean and Adriatic spheres.

    Alongside the Byzantine campaigns, Milutin managed the threat from Bulgarian feudal warlords in the northeast. At the end of the 1290s, two Bulgarian lords — Darman and Kudelin — were jointly ruling the Braničevo region and often attacking the lands of his brother Stefan Dragutin. In 1291, Milutin and Dragutin joined forces against them, securing the northern frontier. The cumulative effect of these campaigns was the annexation of a vast swathe of Macedonian territory, including Skopje, Tetovo, Veles, Štip, Ohrid, and Prizren — cities with substantial Greek-speaking populations and deep Byzantine institutional, ecclesiastical, and cultural roots.

    Much of that was brought to a close with the Serbo-Byzantine peace treaty of 1299, which recognised the new realities of Serbian expansion into Macedonia. The agreement was sealed by a dynastic marriage between the king and Emperor Andronikos's minor daughter Simonida. Simonida was five years old and Milutin was almost fifty, had been married three times, and had adult children. The negotiations were conducted by the Byzantine minister Theodore Metochites; Church circles in Constantinople opposed the marriage, but the emperor was determined to push the deal through. The marriage was celebrated in Thessaloniki in spring 1299, and as a wedding present the Byzantines recognised Serbian rule north of the line Ohrid–Prilep–Štip — a formal recognition by Constantinople of territorial losses it had been unable to reverse militarily, dressed in the language of dynastic alliance.

    The marriage to Simonida, however politically calculated, had profound cultural consequences. It brought the emperor's daughter — and with her a retinue of Greek courtiers, craftsmen, and ecclesiastical advisors — into the heart of the Serbian kingdom at the precise moment when Milutin was embarking on his most ambitious programme of church building. The Byzantine imperial culture she embodied found immediate expression in the art that would define the reign.

    The peace with Byzantium paradoxically destabilised Milutin's relationship with his own brother. Disputes began between them after 1299, and war broke out, lasting with sporadic cease-fires until Dragutin's death in 1316. The conflict had dynastic roots: the agreement at Deževo in 1282 had implicitly promised that Dragutin's line would inherit the throne if Milutin died without heirs, but Milutin's surviving sons and his new Byzantine queen altered the succession calculus. By 1309, Milutin appointed his son, future king Stefan Dečanski, as governor of Zeta — signalling that Dečanski, not Dragutin's son Stefan Vladislav II, was to be heir. This decision provoked Dečanski's own subsequent revolt, and Milutin ordered his son blinded and exiled to Constantinople as punishment — a sentence later apparently reversed, since Dečanski was said to have miraculously recovered his sight and eventually inherited the throne on Milutin's death in 1321.

    Economic transformation was one of Milutin's most consequential legacies. During his reign, Serbian economic power grew rapidly, mostly due to the development of mining. He founded Novo Brdo, which became an internationally important silver mining site. Saxon miners introduced efficient techniques and a legal system that granted them greater autonomy; after fifty years, the Novo Brdo mine became the most prosperous in medieval Serbia and housed a state mint that produced the most silver in the country. Other important sites expanded under his reign included Trepča and Janjevo, and by the fifteenth century Serbia and Bosnia together produced more than twenty percent of all the silver in Europe.

    King Milutin started minting his own money, producing imitations of Venetian coins (grosso), which gradually diminished in value. This led to the ban of these coins by the Republic of Venice and provided King Milutin a place in Dante's Divina Commedia — placed among the falsifiers of coin in the Purgatorio, a detail that registers the impact of his debasement policy on the wider Mediterranean trading economy as far as fourteenth-century Florence.

    It is as a builder and patron of the arts — above all as a ktetor, a founder of churches — that Milutin left his most enduring mark on cultural history. His biographer Archbishop Danilo II records that Milutin founded forty churches and monastic institutions in Serbia, Constantinople, Mount Athos, Thessaloniki, and even in Jerusalem and the monastery of Mount Sinai. Six of the most important survive in Serbia and the former Yugoslav space, together constituting one of the supreme collections of Palaiologan monumental painting anywhere in the Orthodox world.

    The principal monuments include: Bogorodica Ljeviška, Prizren (1306–1307), with frescoes by the Byzantine painters Michael Astrapas and Eutychios, where Milutin is represented in full Byzantine costume with a Byzantine crown — a political statement suggesting his intention to supplant the ruling Byzantine emperor; St. George, Staro Nagoričino (1316–1318), whose monumental decoration was signed twice by the Greek painter Michael Astrapas, most probably of Thessaloniki; the King's Church, Studenica (1314), whose frescoes by Mihailo Astrapas and his workshop are among the finest examples of the Palaiologan Renaissance on Serbian soil; and Gračanica Monastery (completed 1321), whose ktetor's composition shows Christ sending crowns to King Milutin and Queen Simonis in an iconographic concept previously reserved for Byzantine emperors.

    Gračanica also contains one of the most significant innovations in Serbian medieval iconography. The Nemanjić Family Tree — known only in Serbian churches and appearing here for the first time — depicted the entire dynasty rooted in Stefan Nemanja and flowering upwards toward Milutin himself, a powerful visual argument for dynastic legitimacy and divine favour based on compositions of the Tree of Jesse. It would be imitated by his successors throughout the fourteenth century.

    The adoption of the Byzantine artistic idiom was not merely aesthetic but theological and political. By commissioning Thessalonian Greek painters to decorate his foundations in the Palaiologan style, Milutin placed his kingdom within the cultural horizon of Constantinople. His court adopted Byzantine court titles, ceremonial dress, and iconographic programmes for royal portraiture — depicting him consistently in imperial costume, receiving crowns from angels or carrying church models, in a visual rhetoric that claimed imperial status for the Serbian king even as he acknowledged the emperor in Constantinople as his father-in-law.

    Stefan Uroš II Milutin died on 29 October 1321. He was initially buried in the Bulgarian capital Sofia, where his remains were translated in 1460 to the St. Nedelya Cathedral. After his death, disputes over the succession between his son Stefan Konstantin and Stefan Dečanski resulted in civil war, from which Dečanski emerged victorious, crowned king in January 1322. As with most of the Nemanjić monarchs, Milutin was proclaimed a saint by the Serbian Orthodox Church, with a feast day on 30 October — a recognition not only of his personal piety but of his monumental contribution to the Church: forty foundations across the Orthodox world, the introduction of the Palaiologan style to Serbian sacred art, and a reign that had made Serbia the dominant Orthodox kingdom of the Balkans at a moment when Byzantium itself was in terminal decline.

T

  1. The Rabbula Gospels (Rabbula Evangeliarium)

    The Rabbula Gospels (Rabbula Evangeliarium; Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, cod. Plut. I, 56) is one of the most extraordinary illuminated manuscripts to survive from Late Antiquity, a sixth-century Syriac Gospel Book that stands at a pivotal crossroads between Eastern and Western Christian art, between Hellenistic naturalism and the formative language of Byzantine iconography. For any student of medieval manuscript illumination, it is an indispensable reference point.

    The manuscript was completed in 586 at the Monastery of Saint John in Beth Zagba (Beth Zagba), a location long thought to be in northern Mesopotamia but now more convincingly placed in the hinterland between Antioch and Apamea in northern Syria. This relocation is significant because it situates the codex within the cultural orbit of Antioch, helping explain its classical visual references. The monastery itself is described in tradition as a major complex of four spacious churches whose facades faced a central octagon containing a venerated relic.

    The codex is written on parchment. Its folios now measure about 34 x 27 cm, though they were likely larger before repeated rebinding and trimming. It contains 291 folios. The Gospel text, beginning at Matthew 1:23 (so the opening of Matthew is lost), is in the Syriac Peshitta, the standard Syriac biblical translation. It is copied in Estrangela script, a prestigious early Syriac book hand, written right-to-left, so the codex is physically structured opposite to Latin and Greek books.

    The manuscript's name derives from a colophon near the end (folio 291r), where the scribe identifies himself as Rabbula and records date and place. Beyond that line, nothing certain is known about him: his rank, origins, or whether he also painted the miniatures. Some scholars have proposed that scribe and miniaturist could be the same person, but this remains unproven. The colophon is written in the same Estrangela script as the Gospel text, in a smaller hand, securely connecting the dated signature to the main codex.

    Modern scholarship shows that the Rabbula Gospels in its present form is a composite object assembled over time, probably into its current binding in the fifteenth or sixteenth century. It contains three main sections: twenty-six illustrated parchment pages with full-page miniatures and canon tables preceding the Gospel text; a set of twelfth-century paper leaves with liturgical readings (lectionary material); and the principal parchment body of the Peshitta Gospels copied in 586. This composite history means the image cycle and the Gospel text may not have been conceived as one unified project from the beginning.

    The codex's fame rests chiefly on its pictorial cycle, attributed to an anonymous miniaturist or workshop distinct from the named scribe. Most decoration is concentrated in the opening folios and includes full-page miniatures together with Eusebian canon tables framed by elaborate arcades. The canon tables, based on Eusebius of Caesarea's fourth-century concordance system, are enriched with columns, arches, vegetal motifs, birds, deer, rabbits, and prophet and evangelist imagery.

    Stylistically, the miniatures favor saturated color, energetic movement, and strong narrative drama. Certain figures retain draped postures inherited from Hellenistic art, while the ornamental vocabulary often reflects eastern decorative traditions, including interlace and patterned architectural framing, yielding a visual language distinct from contemporary Latin manuscripts.

    The Crucifixion (folio 13a) is one of the most historically significant images in Christian art and is widely regarded as the earliest surviving Crucifixion in an illuminated manuscript. Christ appears alive and open-eyed, clothed in a long sleeveless tunic (colobium), in keeping with early eastern Christus Triumphans conventions. The scene includes the thieves, soldiers casting lots, the Virgin and John, and associated narrative details.

    The Ascension (folio 13b) is equally ambitious: Christ rises in a mandorla, accompanied by symbolic imagery of the four living creatures associated with the Evangelists. Below, the apostles gather while the Virgin appears in an orant pose. The personified sun and moon point to continued dialogue with classical visual memory in sixth-century Syria.

    The manuscript also includes an early monumental Pentecost and a rare scene of the Apostles choosing Matthias to replace Judas (Acts 1), an episode seldom foregrounded in later medieval art. On folio 12r, Judas is depicted hanging from a tree, a stark example of the cycle's narrative directness.

    The codex preserves notes in Syriac, Arabic, and Garshuni (Arabic written in Syriac script), documenting its long life across multiple linguistic communities. A section of liturgical indices in East Syriac script (folios 15v-19r) indicates continued use in public worship.

    Its post-586 history is obscure until the medieval period. An inscription on folio 292v records a donation to the Church of Saint George after the death of Romano, "a priest and visitor from Antioch," suggesting movement from monastic to parish or urban church context, likely in the eleventh or twelfth century. A dated note of 15 May 1361 places the manuscript at the Monastery of Qannubin in Lebanon, seat of the Maronite Patriarchate in the Qadisha Valley. In the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century, the codex was brought to the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana in Florence, where it remains today as cod. Plut. I, 56. Around this final phase, the three sections were assembled in their current form, and some retouching may have occurred.

    The Rabbula Gospels holds a singular place in the history of Christian illumination. Few luxuriously illustrated sixth-century manuscripts survive. Its cycle preserves essential evidence for Christian image-making in the eastern Mediterranean on the eve of the Islamic conquests. The manuscript demonstrates a synthesis of Hellenistic figural language, near-eastern ornamental abstraction, and emergent Byzantine theological iconography. For this reason, it is not a peripheral curiosity but a central witness for later Byzantine, Coptic, Armenian, and medieval Latin manuscript traditions.

  2. Thomas Aquinas

    Thomas Aquinas was born at Roccasecca, near Aquino, in what was then the Kingdom of Sicily (present-day Lazio, Italy), around 1225. He was born to the most powerful branch of the d'Aquino family. His father, Landulf VI of Aquino, Lord of Roccasecca, was a miles in the service of Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor. Thomas's mother, Theodora Galluccio, Countess of Teano, belonged to the Rossi branch of the Neapolitan Caracciolo family. Through his maternal lineage, Thomas was distantly related to the Hohenstaufen imperial dynasty, and to the royal houses of Aragon, Castile, and France.

    The geopolitical context of his birth was turbulent. The Kingdom of Sicily was governed by Frederick II, who was in almost continual conflict with the papacy. The d'Aquino family's position, loyal to the Emperor yet deeply Catholic, placed Thomas from birth at the intersection of the great powers of medieval Christendom, a tension that would define not only his childhood but, in sublimated form, his entire intellectual project.

    Thomas Aquinas spent most of his childhood in the Benedictine monastery at Monte Cassino, where his parents placed him as a prospective monk when he was about five years old. The family's intention was explicit: as the youngest son, Thomas was destined for an ecclesiastical career of prestige, ideally as abbot of Monte Cassino itself, one of the oldest and most venerable monasteries in Christendom, founded by Saint Benedict in the sixth century. The oblation of a child to such an institution was both a religious act and a dynastic strategy: it secured the family's spiritual patronage while providing Thomas with the finest available education.

    He remained at Monte Cassino for nine years, receiving a thorough grounding in the liberal arts, Latin, Scripture, and the patristic tradition. When he was fifteen, Emperor Frederick II took over the monastery and the monks and students had to leave, so Thomas went to the University of Naples. At Naples, one of the few European universities founded by a secular ruler rather than the Church, and consequently more open to heterodox currents of thought, Thomas encountered two forces that would reshape the entire direction of his life. The first was Aristotle: the texts of the Greek philosopher, newly translated into Latin through Arabic intermediary versions, were beginning to circulate in the European schools with the force of intellectual revelation, reopening fundamental questions about the nature of reality, knowledge, and the cosmos that the Platonic-Augustinian tradition had settled too comfortably. The second was the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans, whose friars, committed to lives of radical poverty, study, and apostolic preaching, embodied a form of religious dedication wholly unlike the wealthy Benedictine monasticism his family had planned for him.

    In 1244, at approximately nineteen years of age, Thomas secretly joined the Dominican Order at Naples. When his family found out, they felt so betrayed that he had turned his back on the principles to which they subscribed that they decided to kidnap him. The prospect of a nobleman of the d'Aquino line embracing the life of a mendicant friar, begging, wandering, preaching to the poor, was, to his family, a social catastrophe of the first order. The Dominicans were a new kind of religious institution, barely a generation old, and their conspicuous poverty was associated not with the honorable withdrawal of traditional monasticism but with a subversive assault on established hierarchies.

    In an attempt to prevent Theodora's interference in Thomas's choice, the Dominicans arranged for Thomas to be removed to Rome and then to Paris. However, on the way to Rome, his brothers who were soldiers under Emperor Frederick, following their mother's instructions, seized him as he was drinking from a spring near the town of Acquapendente and took him back to his parents, who were then at the castle of Monte San Giovanni Campano.

    He was held in the family homes at Monte San Giovanni and Roccasecca in an attempt to prevent him from assuming the Dominican habit and to convince him to become a Benedictine. Political concerns prevented the Pope from ordering Thomas's release, which extended his detention, during which he spent time tutoring his sisters and communicating with members of the Dominican Order. The family's desperation escalated: his brothers, as tradition records, arranged for a young woman to enter his chamber and tempt him into sexual sin, which, had it succeeded, would have made him ineligible for the priesthood. Thomas, according to every source, seized a burning brand from the hearth and drove her out, then fell to his knees in prayer. The tradition adds that two angels appeared to him that night and girded him with a cord of chastity, a grace he was said to have felt physically for the rest of his life.

    After nearly two years of detention, his family relented. Teodora and her daughters saw that further attempts to change Thomas's resolve were useless and allowed him to rejoin the friars in Naples, from whence he was sent to Paris.

    Arriving at the Dominican priory of Saint-Jacques in Paris around October 1245, Thomas began his formal theological studies under the greatest natural philosopher of the age: the celebrated Saint Albert the Great. It was Albert, Albertus Magnus, who had made it his life's mission to assimilate the whole of Aristotelian philosophy into the framework of Christian thought, commenting on virtually every work of the Stagirite with encyclopedic thoroughness. Under Albert's tutelage, Thomas received not only a comprehensive education in Aristotelian science, metaphysics, and ethics, but also the intellectual method, patient, rigorous, comprehensive, that would define his own mature work.

    The relationship between master and pupil became one of the great intellectual partnerships of the medieval period. Thomas's sheer physical size and his characteristic silence in disputations had misled his fellow students into dismissing him as slow-witted, they called him the "Dumb Ox of Sicily." Albert corrected this misperception with a prophecy that has become one of the most famous utterances in the history of education: "We call him the dumb ox, but in his teaching he will one day produce such a bellowing that it will be heard throughout the world."

    Albert brought Thomas with him when he was appointed to establish a new studium generale at Cologne, where Thomas continued his studies and was ordained as a priest around 1250. After four years as a bachelor of theology, lecturing on the Bible and on Peter Lombard's Sentences, Aquinas received his doctorate and was immediately appointed master of theology, once again at an earlier age than the statutes officially allowed.

    From 1256 until 1259, Thomas held the Dominican chair of theology in Paris, preaching, lecturing on the Bible, and presiding over various philosophical and theological disputations. This was the most intellectually charged environment in Europe. The University of Paris was the supreme arena of scholastic controversy, where Dominicans, Franciscans, secular masters, and Augustinian Hermits competed for intellectual prestige and institutional authority. Thomas quickly established himself as one of the dominant presences among the mendicant masters, not through aggression but through the extraordinary clarity, precision, and comprehensiveness of his thought.

    The central intellectual challenge of his era was the arrival of the full Aristotelian corpus in Latin translation, much of it channeled through Arabic commentators, above all Averroes (Ibn Rushd) of Cordoba, whose radical interpretations of Aristotle threatened to dissolve the boundary between philosophy and theology entirely. Some of the Averroist theses, particularly the doctrine of the unity of the intellect, which seemed to deny individual immortality, were incompatible with Christian doctrine. Thomas's response was neither to reject Aristotle (as some conservatives wished) nor to follow Averroes in his most radical conclusions (as the Latin Averroists at Paris were doing), but to reread Aristotle more carefully and argue that a correct interpretation of the philosopher was fully compatible with Christian faith.

    It was also during this period that Thomas began work on the Summa contra gentiles, a systematic theological treatise written not for university students but, initially, as a handbook for Dominican missionaries engaged in apologetic disputes with Muslims, Jews, and heretical Christians in North Africa and Spain. This treatise was completed after he returned to Italy to lecture at the papal court in 1261.

    From 1259 to 1268, Thomas served at various locations in Italy, Orvieto, Rome, Viterbo, attached to the papal court as its resident theologian. These years were among the most productive of his life. He enjoyed the direct patronage of successive popes, access to the finest libraries, and the leisure to develop his thought without the constant pressure of university disputations.

    It was in Rome, around 1265, that Thomas began the work that would become the crowning achievement of medieval theology: the Summa Theologiae. He began his masterwork while he was in Rome, teaching Dominican students. The Summa was conceived as a comprehensive, systematic account of the whole of Christian doctrine, organized in a characteristic dialectical method: each article poses a question, states objections to the correct answer, gives the correct answer (responsio), and then replies to each objection in turn. The structure is both pedagogically efficient and intellectually elegant, allowing the reader to understand not only what Thomas thought but why he thought it and what considerations he was weighing.

    The architecture of the Summa is tripartite. The first part (Prima Pars) treats God, the divine nature, the Trinity, creation, and the angels. The second part, divided into two (Prima Secundae and Secunda Secundae), is a comprehensive ethics: the nature of human happiness, the passions, virtues and vices, law, grace, and the specific moral theology of the Christian life. The third part (Tertia Pars) treats Christ, the Incarnation, and the sacraments. Among its best-known contents are the Five Ways (Quinque Viae), Thomas's famous arguments for God's existence, natural law theory, virtue ethics, and sacramental theology.

    It was also during these Italian years that Thomas was commissioned by Pope Urban IV to compose the liturgical texts for the newly instituted feast of Corpus Christi, the celebration of the Eucharist. The result was a set of hymns and antiphons, including the Pange Lingua, Tantum Ergo, and O Salutaris Hostia, that are still sung throughout the Catholic world. As a poet, he wrote some of the most gravely beautiful eucharistic hymns in the Church's liturgy.

    When his second four-year term in Paris came to an end he returned to Italy, but between 1269 and 1272 Thomas was recalled to Paris for a second stint, and this period was the most fiercely combative of his career. He was now fighting on two fronts simultaneously. Against the radical Averroists, above all Siger of Brabant, he argued that the doctrine of the unity of the intellect was philosophically indefensible even on Aristotle's own terms. Against conservative Augustinians, led partly by Franciscan masters, he defended his use of Aristotelian philosophy against charges of innovation and heterodoxy.

    Aquinas was also heavily influenced by Augustine's integration of Christian theology with Neoplatonism, particularly regarding the nature of God and the soul. He also drew inspiration from Islamic and Jewish thinkers such as Avicenna, Averroes, and Maimonides. His intellectual generosity, his willingness to learn from Muslim and Jewish philosophers, to follow Aristotle wherever the argument led, to grant the strongest possible formulation to his opponents before refuting them, was itself a kind of intellectual courage remarkable for its age.

    The Five Ways, presented in the opening questions of the Prima Pars of the Summa, distill this synthesis into five tightly argued demonstrations of God's existence from natural reason alone. The First Way reasons from motion to an Unmoved Mover; the Second from efficient causation to an Uncaused First Cause; the Third from contingent beings to a Necessary Being; the Fourth from degrees of perfection to an absolute standard; and the Fifth from the teleological order of nature to an intelligent designer. None of these arguments was invented by Thomas, they have roots in Aristotle, Avicenna, and earlier Christian thinkers, but his formulation of them was precise, economical, and compelling enough to make them the standard reference points for all subsequent natural theology.

    In 1272, Thomas returned to Naples, where he established a new Dominican studium and continued simultaneously his enormous commentary series on Aristotle and the composition of the Summa. He was nearing completion of the final portion in December 1273.

    Then, on the feast of Saint Nicholas, 6 December 1273, something happened at Mass in the Dominican church of San Domenico Maggiore in Naples that has never been fully explained. Aquinas had a mystical experience while celebrating Mass on December 6, 1273, after which he stopped writing, leaving his great work, the Summa Theologiae, unfinished. When asked why he had stopped writing, Aquinas replied: "I cannot go on. All that I have written seems to me like so much straw compared to what I have seen and what has been revealed to me."

    He used the remainder of December 1273 to recover at his sister Theodora's house. Nonetheless, Thomas still had his wits about him, for not only was he able to carry on a conversation until the end of his life, but two months later he composed one precious last piece of theological writing, a brief exposition on the relation of human freedom and divine foreknowledge for the monks at Monte Cassino.

    The Summa was never completed. What Thomas left unfinished, the treatment of penance, extreme unction, holy orders, matrimony, and the last things, was subsequently compiled by his disciples, primarily from his earlier commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, and appended as the Supplementum.

    Early in 1274, the Pope directed Thomas to attend the Second Council of Lyons, and though far from well, he undertook the journey. On the way he stopped at the castle of a niece and there became seriously ill. He wished to end his days in a monastery and not being able to reach a house of the Dominicans, he was taken to the Cistercians. He died at the monastery of Fossanova, one mile from Sonnino, on March 7, 1274. He was forty-nine years old.

    His last recorded words, spoken before receiving the Eucharist for the final time, were: "I receive Thee, price of my soul's redemption, I receive Thee, viaticum of my pilgrimage, for whose love I have studied, watched, labored; I have preached Thee, I have taught Thee." He submitted all his writings to the judgment of the Church, asking that whatever in them was erroneous be corrected.

  3. Thomas of Celano

    Thomas of Celano — in Italian Tommaso da Celano — was a Franciscan friar, hagiographer, and poet, best known as the principal biographer of Saint Francis of Assisi and the probable author of the Dies Irae, one of the most celebrated Latin sequences of the medieval liturgy. His writings constitute the earliest and most authoritative documentary sources for the life of Francis, making him an indispensable figure for anyone studying thirteenth-century Italian religious culture and hagiography.

    Thomas was born around 1185–1190 into the noble family of the Conti dei Marsi at Celano, a town in the Abruzzi region of central Italy. He received a thorough liberal arts education, possibly at the Benedictine monastery of Saint John the Baptist near his hometown, which gave him the intellectual formation necessary for the sophisticated Latin prose he would later produce. He joined the Order of Friars Minor around 1215, during the lifetime of Francis himself, and developed a personal acquaintance with the saint that would lend an eyewitness dimension to his later biographical writing.

    In 1221, Thomas was sent to Germany alongside Caesarius of Speyer to expand and consolidate the Franciscan presence in the German-speaking lands — one of the order's most ambitious early missionary ventures. He proved an effective administrator and was appointed custos (guardian) responsible for the convents of Cologne, Mainz, Worms, and Speyer, and subsequently became Caesarius's vicar in governing the entire German province. He returned to Italy before September 1223 and remained there for the rest of his life, maintaining close proximity to Francis in the saint's final years.

    Thomas produced three major hagiographical works on Francis of Assisi, all written on commission and constituting a unique documentary corpus on the founder of the Franciscan order.

    The Vita Prima (Vita Beati Francisci), completed by 1230, was commissioned directly by Pope Gregory IX shortly after Francis's canonization in 1228. It is structured in three uneven parts: the first covers Francis's youth, conversion, and the founding of the order up to 1223; the second describes the final two years of his life, his reception of the stigmata on Mount La Verna on 14 September 1224 (the first human recorded to have borne the marks of Christ's Passion), and his death in 1226; the third recounts the canonization and early miracles. The work draws on eyewitness testimony and is imbued with the theological framework of the saint as a perfect alter Christus.

    The Vita Secunda, compiled between 1244 and 1247 on the commission of Crescentius of Jesi, then Minister General of the order, functions as a supplement rather than a replacement of the first biography. It incorporates new materials gathered from the direct companions of Francis — notably Brother Leo and Rufinus of Assisi — and reflects the evolving internal debates within the Franciscan order about the true interpretation of Francis's ideal of poverty. A third work, a treatise on the Miracles of Saint Francis, was written around 1254–1257 at the request of Blessed John of Parma, Crescentius's successor as Minister General.

    Thomas has long been considered the author of the Dies Irae ("Day of Wrath"), the great eschatological sequence describing the Last Judgment that became the standard sequence of the Tridentine Requiem Mass. Its authorship, however, remains uncertain and is debated by modern scholars. He also traditionally receives credit for the earliest Life of Saint Clare of Assisi, though this attribution too is not universally accepted. Regardless of these disputes, his Latin prose and verse demonstrate exceptional literary mastery and a deep command of the Augustinian and Bernardine spiritual tradition.

    In 1260, Thomas retired to his last post as spiritual director to a convent of Poor Clares (Clarisses) in Tagliacozzo, in his native Abruzzi. He died there sometime between 1260 and 1270, and was initially buried in the church of San Giovanni Val dei Varri; his remains were later translated to the church of San Francesco in Tagliacozzo, where they rest today. A process for his beatification was formally opened in Avezzano, and in 1991 the Congregation for the Causes of Saints declared the process valid and opened the Roman Phase, granting him the title Servant of God.

    For scholars of medieval hagiography, Franciscan history, and Italian religious culture, Thomas of Celano's writings are primary sources of the highest order. His biographies shaped the visual and literary image of Francis that artists — from Cimabue and Giotto onward — translated into the great fresco cycles of Assisi and beyond. His precise descriptions of Francis's spiritual experiences, physical appearance, and miraculous deeds provided the iconographic materia from which the entire tradition of Franciscan art drew its narrative vocabulary.

U

  1. Urban IV (Jacques Pantaleon)

    Pope Urban IV (Jacques Pantaleon; c. 1195-2 October 1264) reigned for barely three years, never once set foot in Rome as pope, and yet did two things that outlasted him: he instituted the feast of Corpus Christi, and he invited Charles of Anjou into Italy, setting in motion the destruction of the Hohenstaufen and the reorientation of the peninsula's politics for a century.

    He was born at Troyes in Champagne, probably in the closing years of the twelfth century. c. 1195 is the usual estimate, though c. 1200 is also given, and no source is decisive. The tradition that he was the son of a cobbler (sutor) is repeated by the older literature and is plausible for a career made entirely through university and curial service rather than birth; it should nonetheless be labelled tradition rather than documented fact. He studied at Paris (theology and law), and accounts diverge on whether he then taught canon law there. Britannica asserts it, the Catholic Encyclopedia does not, and the professorship should be treated as uncertain.

    His career was that of a competent northern French cleric who became useful to popes. He held a canonry at Laon and became archdeacon of Liège, later archdeacon of Laon. At Liège, in the 1240s, he encountered the eucharistic devotion of Juliana of Mont-Cornillon and the diocesan feast of Corpus Christi ordered by Bishop Robert de Thourotte in 1246, the single most important fact in his biography for the Bolsena question. He came to the notice of Innocent IV at the First Council of Lyon (1245), and was sent on missions to Germany, where he worked at ecclesiastical discipline in Silesia and at the long conflict between the Teutonic Knights and their Prussian subjects, a process that culminated in the Treaty of Christburg (usually dated 1249, sometimes 1248). In 1251 he was in northern Germany recruiting support for William of Holland, the papal candidate for the Empire. He was made bishop of Verdun in 1253 and Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem in 1255 by Alexander IV, an office by then largely titular in a kingdom reduced to a coastal strip.

    He was at Viterbo, seeking western aid for the Holy Land, when Alexander IV died on 25 May 1261. The Sacred College then numbered only eight cardinals, and after a three-month deadlock they chose the patriarch, a man outside their own body. Urban was the first pope elected without being a cardinal; only five would follow him (Gregory X, Celestine V, Clement V, Urban V, Urban VI). He was crowned on 4 September 1261 at Santa Maria a Gradi in Viterbo. He immediately addressed the smallness of the College by creating fourteen cardinals, among them Simon de Brion (the future Martin IV) and Guy Foulques (the future Clement IV), an act with consequences well beyond his lifetime, and one that decisively strengthened the French element in the curia.

    A fortnight before his election, Constantinople had fallen to Michael VIII Palaiologos and the Latin Empire had ended. Urban attempted, without success, to raise a crusade for its restoration. Pachymeres reports that he had one of Michael's envoys flayed alive, a hostile Greek source and a claim that deserves caution typical of atrocity anecdotes in polemical historiography. His more consequential eastern initiative was intellectual: he commissioned Thomas Aquinas, then attached to the papal court at Orvieto, to write the Contra errores Graecorum (1263), and it was to Urban that Aquinas dedicated the Catena aurea.

    The pontificate's political substance was the Sicilian question. Manfred, illegitimate son of Frederick II, held the kingdom (a papal fief), and his influence extended into Lombardy and Tuscany. Urban renewed his excommunication and sought a counter-king, offering the crown successively to Louis IX's brother, to Edmund of England, and finally, in 1263, to Charles of Anjou, count of Provence and Louis IX's brother. The terms Urban imposed are revealing: Sicily was never to be united to the Empire; its king would swear fealty, pay an annual tribute (10,000 ounces of gold), and abstain from acquiring substantial dominion in northern Italy or the Papal States. Meanwhile Urban simultaneously negotiated with Manfred, dangling papal recognition in exchange for help against Byzantium, a double game he sustained for two years. Whether this was cynicism or prudence by a weak power with two irons in the fire remains debated. Fearing assassination plots and a converging Ghibelline attack, he moved from Orvieto to Perugia in 1264.

    Between those two Umbrian residences falls the event for which he is popularly remembered. On 11 August 1264, at Orvieto, he issued the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo, extending the feast of Corpus Christi to the universal Church, to be kept on the Thursday after the octave of Pentecost, arguably the first papally mandated universal feast of the Latin rite. The office and hymns, including Pange lingua, are traditionally ascribed to Aquinas; the attribution was long doubted and is now broadly, though not universally, accepted on the strength of early Dominican liturgical manuscripts. What must be stressed, since the two are often conflated, is that Transiturus nowhere mentions Bolsena, a miracle, or a corporal. The bull argues from theology and calendar. Urban's motive is fully explained by Liège, where he had watched the feast take shape decades earlier. The link to the Bolsena miracle is a fourteenth-century construction, and any biography that presents the bull as Urban's response to the bleeding host has reversed the causation.

    He fell ill after reaching Perugia and died there on 2 October 1264, before Charles of Anjou ever crossed the Alps. Contemporaries linked his death to the Great Comet of that year, which appeared as he sickened and faded as he died, a coincidence that says more about thirteenth century cosmology than about pathology; no cause of death is recorded. He was buried at Perugia. Clement IV, one of his own creations, carried the Angevin policy through to Manfred's death at Benevento (1266) and Conradin's execution at Naples (1268).

    Two things survive him physically. He began the church of Saint-Urbain at Troyes in 1262, on the site of his father's shop, a rayonnant building of remarkable structural daring. And the corporal of Bolsena, which he almost certainly never heard of, is still carried through Orvieto on the feast he founded.

    He also wandered, unwillingly, into legend: in some versions of the Tannhäuser story it is Urban who refuses absolution and whose dry staff then blossoms. There is nothing behind this in thirteenth-century evidence.

V

  1. Vallombrosan Order

    The Vallombrosan Order, formally the Congregatio Vallis Umbrosae Ordinis Sancti Benedicti (O.S.B. Vall.), is one of the most significant monastic reform congregations to emerge from medieval Italy, rooted in an intense spiritual movement that sought to restore the purity of Benedictine life in an era of widespread ecclesiastical corruption.

    The Order was founded by San Giovanni Gualberto (c. 985-1073), a Florentine nobleman of the Visdomini family. According to Vallombrosan hagiographic tradition, his conversion occurred on Good Friday of 1003, when he renounced vengeance against his brother's murderer - an act of Christian forgiveness that profoundly redirected his life. He subsequently sought a monastic vocation, experimenting first with the Cluniac community of San Miniato al Monte in Florence and later with the Camaldolese hermits, before withdrawing definitively to the dense forest of Vallombrosa, in the Apennine hills southeast of Florence, around 1030-1036.

    The site of Vallombrosa - forested, solitary, and elevated at roughly 3,300 feet above sea level - suited perfectly Giovanni's vision of strict withdrawal from the world. The new community's foundation received formal ecclesiastical recognition with the consecration of its first church by Blessed Rotho, Bishop of Paderborn, in 1038, and the donation of the land by Itta, Abbess of the neighboring monastery of Sant'Ellero, in 1039.

    The spirituality of Vallombrosa was built on a rigorous return to the Regula Benedicti, with a particular emphasis on communal poverty, strict clausura, and the rejection of simony and Nicolaitanism - the two great corruptions plaguing the eleventh-century Church. Giovanni was opposed above all to the buying and selling of ecclesiastical offices and sacraments, and his community became a living protest against clerical worldliness.

    A distinctive institution of the new order was the extensive use of conversi - lay brothers who performed manual labor and external tasks, allowing the choir monks to remain in strict enclosure. The order also refused to provide officials for parish churches and chapels, preserving its communal integrity. The constitutional framework Giovanni envisioned, known as the Vinculum Caritatis (Bond of Charity), organized the monasteries into a congregation in which each house was autonomous and governed by its own abbot, elected by the community with the consent of the Abbot Major of Vallombrosa. The Abbot Major himself was elected by the assembled abbots of all the affiliated houses, who met annually at Vallombrosa with full legislative authority.

    The most dramatic episode in the early history of the order was the ordeal by fire performed by the Vallombrosan monk Blessed Pietro Igneo (Petrus Igneus) at the abbey of Settimo near Florence in February 1068. The event was staged as a divine proof against the simoniac Bishop Pietro Mezzabarba of Florence, and Pietro Igneo reportedly walked through flames unharmed, inflaming popular devotion and drawing enormous attention to the Vallombrosan reform cause. The episode earned the order both papal favor and widespread public sympathy, consolidating its moral authority throughout Tuscany.

    Formal papal protection came in stages: Pope Victor II confirmed the order in 1056, and a bull of Urban II in 1090 enumerated fifteen monasteries besides the motherhouse. A bull of Paschal II in 1115 listed twelve more, and under Anastasius IV and Adrian IV (1153-1156) a further twenty-four were added. By the pontificate of Innocent III (early thirteenth century), the congregation counted over sixty monasteries, all situated in Italy, with a notable presence in Sardinia where the order administered wealthy monasteries and governed numerous rural villages.

    The period from the foundation to the early fourteenth century represents the true eta d'oro of Vallombrosan monasticism. The congregation expanded throughout central and northern Italy, radiating from its Tuscan heartland into Lombardy, Liguria, and the Veneto, as well as into Sardinia. By 1160, Vallombrosan monks were present in fifty-seven monasteries. The annual chapter at Vallombrosa - where all abbots gathered with legislative power - maintained cohesion across the growing network and ensured the circulation of monks between houses, sustaining a uniform observance.

    Among the order's most distinguished early figures was Bernardo degli Uberti, the superior general who, under the impulse of Popes Gregory VII, Urban II, and Paschal II, gave definitive structural form to the congregation as a fully recognized branch of the Benedictine family. The movement only began to be formally described as "Vallombrosan" in sources from around 1080.

    The fourteenth century brought difficulties common to much of European monasticism: the catastrophe of the Black Death (1348), internal weakening, and above all the corrosive system of commenda, by which secular or absentee abbots were appointed by external authority, draining monastic revenues and disrupting communal life. The institution of the Abbot Major gradually lost much of its authority, and the congregation's expansion halted.

    A decisive reform came in 1540, when the Vallombrosans, having suffered extensively from the effects of commenda, adopted the constitutions of the Cassinese Congregation of Saint Justina of Padua, including the exchange of their traditional grey wool habit for a black garb. The reform abolished the system of life-term abbots and replaced it with three-year terms, while the office of superior general ceased to be identified with the Abbot of Vallombrosa and became instead a titular abbot serving four-year terms alongside four definitors.

    From 1662 to 1680, the Vallombrosan congregation was briefly united with the Sylvestrine order, a union that proved temporary. The monastery of Vallombrosa itself was enriched by the construction works of Abbot Nicolini in 1637 and saw the establishment of an astronomical observatory in 1634.

    The Napoleonic era struck a severe blow: in 1808, French troops plundered Vallombrosa and the monastery was left deserted until 1815. The final suppression came with the unified Italian state: in 1866, the Italian government suppressed the monastery under the laws dissolving religious houses. The abbey buildings were converted in 1870 into Italy's first school of forestry, modeled on German institutions, and the site also became a mountain health resort.

    Despite the suppression of 1866, a small community of monks survived to care for the church and maintain a meteorological station at Vallombrosa. The order was not extinguished: the Vallombrosan congregation persisted and eventually regrouped, and it continues to exist today as a living branch of the Benedictine family. In June 2025, Pope Leo XIV formally addressed the Vallombrosan congregation, underscoring its continuing significance within the Catholic Church.

    The Vallombrosans' legacy extends well beyond their institutional history.
